Talanov:

At the XXII International Conference on Socionics, St. Petersburg psychophysiologist V.L. Talanov in his report “Content and physiological interpretation of socionic features “constructivists-emotivists”, “tacticians-strategists”, “compliant-stubborn” and “careless-prudent” spoke about his own vision of model “A”, using psychophysiological, and not psychological terminology, as is done in socionics. Based on the results of his experiments, he emphasized that there are not eight, but only four generalized socionic functions, but each, unlike the canonical model “A”, is characterized by two parameters, namely, thresholds for excitation and inhibition.

For high and low thresholds, the zones of optimal intensity for them of signals do not intersect, the thresholds turn out to be filters capable of passing through themselves either only strong-signal or only weak-signal stimulation. The excitation channel of a function has both an input (excitation of the function by signals: its own or from other functions) and an output (generation of a signal for transmission to another function or to another individual), and the inhibition channel has only an input. A high excitation threshold corresponds to the extroversion of a given function in terms of its energy consumption and specialization in strong incoming and outgoing signals, and a low threshold corresponds to introversion.

If a person is an extrovert, then his first two functions in the traditional first ring of model "A" have a high stimulation threshold, a high level of optimal excitation and a high level of outgoing signals, and the third and fourth have a low one. In introverts, it is the opposite. A high inhibition threshold always corresponds to the "white" color of the functions. V.L. Talanov calls such functions intrathymic, they are characterized by increased inhibition with a high intensity of stimulation from other functions entering the receptor.  Extroverted functions (black) are inhibited, on the contrary, with a weak signal level. Thus, the concepts of extroversion and extrotimacy turn out to be non-coinciding and independent of each other. The color of the functions in the ring alternates, and similarly to its alternation, the height of the inhibition thresholds alternates. The first and fourth functions are always unbalanced in the height of the inhibition and excitation thresholds (high excitation thresholds correspond to low inhibition thresholds and vice versa), and for the third and fourth functions it automatically turns out that the excitation and inhibition thresholds have the same height, that is, these functions are balanced in the psychophysiological sense and can self-regulate even with their own signals, within their own functional sphere. V.L. Talanov's model (model "T") explains in psychophysiological language the nature of the mutual influence of functions within the ring, the features of each of the four functions (for example, the programmatic nature of the first function and the creative - of the second), and also, based on the nature of the interaction of thresholds in the same function, but different TIMs, predicts the features of intertype relations that arise in practice. For example, the complete model of Don Quixote, according to Talanov (model "T"), will look like the following formula:

- for the unbalanced ILE subtype.

In these formulas, the left upper index next to the function indicates the optimal threshold of its excitation (b - high, m - low), the right lower index with the same designations indicates the optimal threshold of inhibition. I - intuition, L - logic, S - sensorics, E - ethics. The fraction in brackets before the formula shows the general properties of the strength-weakness of the individual's nervous system in excitation (in the numerator) and inhibition (in the denominator).

The letter b (high thresholds) corresponds to the strong, and m (low thresholds) to the weak.

In contrast to the particular (partial) properties of the nervous system, expressed by indices at the functions and related to each function separately, the general properties equally affect all functions of the individual. In this case, the action of those partial functional channels whose threshold height coincides with the corresponding threshold of the general property of the nervous system is facilitated; in addition, there is also a certain shift of partial thresholds towards general ones. Therefore, the indication of the general property of the strength-weakness of the nervous system in excitation by the index in the numerator of the fraction specifies which of the two unbalanced functions of ILE will be the program one (the one whose excitation threshold coincides with the index of the general property of the nervous system). The index in the denominator of the fraction (general strength-weakness in inhibition), interacting with the lower indices of the functions, forms the accentuation of the type and specifies the subtype.

Regardless of the subtype, ILE's intuition, in accordance with the given Talanov model, is strong-signal in excitation and weak-signal in inhibition. All other functions are assessed similarly.

If we now take a model "T" of some other type, for example, EIE, then it will not be difficult to describe the nature of the interaction of the two mental structures. EIE's intuition is capable of exciting ILE’s intuition, and vice versa, because both have a strong-signal intuition in excitation. However, EIE's intuition is not capable of inhibiting ILE's intuition, because this requires a low, not a high signal. At the same time, ILE's intuition is capable of both exciting and inhibiting EIE intuition, which can easily be interpreted as the ability to control it. The interactions of all other functions are revealed in a similar way. As a result, a picture of ILE's positive dominance over EIE arises, which is perhaps close to the concept of a socionic order.

Bukalov’s Socionics dimensionality:

Functions are in spaces of different dimensionality, and even in different geographic spaces, since their qualities are different, because, in the end, ethical, logical or sensory parameters are not the same thing. If the concept of space in this case is used conditionally, metaphorically, and not literally, then this can be considered only as an auxiliary tool, generally alien to the conceptual structure of socionics, but, in some sense, useful.

This does not mean at all that the concept of space cannot be applied in socionics.

However, the point is not at all in applying it, but in discovering spatial categories and parameters as inherent in socionic concepts. A.V. Bukalov offers some idea of ​​space, but is it geometrically real or is it just a parametric set called space in the framework of the mathematical-terminological style? Both possibilities remain potentially useful, but clarification of concepts is necessary. A.V. Bukalov's four parameters - experience, norms, situations, and time - constitute a set, the completeness of which is problematic, that is, it is not proven, the elements of this set themselves are not constructed deductively, but discovered empirically, which, of course, is also not bad, but not enough. And, most importantly, the semantics of this set does not follow from the semantics of the model. These parameters are perceived as something plausible, but not obligatory, although empirically registered.

What could represent a geometrically real space of socionic functions?  This could be a hypothetical energy-information space already introduced into scientific circulation, in which, for example, information flows of television programs and telephone conversations are supposedly located.

Although a banal answer suggests itself here that this is simply a space of electromagnetic waves. However, let us consider this issue more closely.

Firstly, in a geometric sense, a set of electromagnetic waves falls under the definition of space, since this is a “place” in which electromagnetic entities are located, and in which they can change their location, or coordinates. But I believe that the psyche relates to another, more general or more subtle energy than electromagnetism. And so, if we admit the existence of an energy-information space based on another, "living" energy, where psychic entities are located, then all socionic reasoning could relate to this space. And then psychic entities become real objects of this space, and not scientific abstractions. And then they cannot be assigned arbitrarily, but must be discovered with all their features, and preferably in a strictly controlled laboratory experiment, and not speculatively. The speculative stage is inevitable, but it must be based on empirics, confirmed by empirics, controlled by empirics and embodied in practically useful technologies. However, the latter has been very successful at the International Institute of Socionics for many years now.

If the psycho-informational space that A.V. Bukalov talks about is real, that is, sooner or later it can be recognized by devices, then the dimensionality of functions, as mental organs, is not a mathematical abstraction, but something real.

And here I assume that the dimensionality of all functions is the same, like, for example, the dimensionality of the organs of the physical body. That is, there are no logical grounds to believe that the dimensions of these organs are different, and what “seems” to us as a difference in productivity, energy consumption or other quantitative parameters of functions, then this may turn out to be a semantic difference, in the sense that the functions have different products, which are subjectively assessed differently.

Bukalov's categories:

Self. Most likely, this is undefinable because it goes into some existential depths. The self is not only the equivalent of integrity, but also the intention to maintain an existential trajectory, that is, the path and history of individual existence. The self as an equivalent of integrity can only be designated. The choice of goal and decision-making are associated with the self. It is the basis and germ of behavior, which can also be understood as the center of subjectivity, the essence of subjectivity and, ultimately, as a subject. If this is so, then the entities behind the concepts of the self and the subject are identical, and their terminological design depends only on inclusion in the corresponding subject area. The subject is from philosophy, and the self is from psychology. The self as an equivalent of an individual, which literally means “indivisible”, but in a different conceptual and terminological design, seems to be something else. But the self is also indivisible. The self as an embryo of independence, but not yet independence. One must grow up to this, mature. This is the existential core. But this is not a definition, this is an attempt to expand the semantic field of the concept of self.

The existential status of the self is unclear - what is it? An entity with physical and spatio-temporal characteristics? A parameter, that is, a measurable property of an object? If the self is a parameter that determines existence-non-existence, then it is unclear how and why it should be put on a par with physically observable quantities - norms and situations. An abstraction that helps to capture some intuitively grasped meaning related to primary identification or self-identification?

Experience:

It seems that experience is what provides the greatest differences between individualities. At the XXII International Conference on Socionics, several of its participants discussed the concept of experience in comparison with the concept of memory.

They roughly agreed that experience is processed memory, although each of the participants in the discussion had their own shades of characterizing the concept of experience. Of course, the concept of experience includes  memory, but there is still a noticeable difference between these concepts. Memory is, first, an information base. Experience is a technologized memory, a mobilized memory, memory in the form of a working tool that a person can use to optimize their behavior.

Norms and situations:

Two categories, apparently having quite a real meaning, which strongly contrasts them with the self, about which it is generally difficult to say anything and compare anything with it, except for synonymous tautologies. But this very contrast is alarming. The fact that these categories belong to the same set as the self requires special justification. Norms can be considered as relatively rigid constants that limit behavior. A norm in this sense presupposes the presence of internal standards and the ability to compare external circumstances with them and the coincidence or deviation of circumstances and the subject's manifestations from the standards. Situations can be understood as variable circumstances that require an adequate reaction. Whom? The Self? The subject? An adequate reaction involves analyzing the situation with subsequent synthesis of behavior.

Time:

A universal physical parameter complementary to the dynamics of an object and comparable to it. The level of abstraction of this category differs greatly from the level of abstraction of the categories of norm and situation, since time acts as a universal argument and, in this sense, controls any entities as functions dependent on it.

And one more thing. Why are these parameters called and depicted as vectors? By definition, a vector is an entity characterized by magnitude and orientation. Let's say we can talk about a time vector, but how can we represent the self as a vector? We can measure time in some units, but how can we measure the self? To represent experience and norms as a vector, we must first agree on the units in which we measure them, and then indicate what their direction is. If time intervals can be represented as adjoining durations, then it is difficult to imagine adjoining norms or units of experience, thus forming a “normative continuum” or a continuum of units of experience. True, one can imagine a certain card index in which cards with “different” norms recorded on them or statements in which personal experience is recorded are placed. Then the unit of measurement of norms can be one such card. But if there can be an infinite number of time intervals, at least theoretically, then an infinite number of norms is something unimaginable. Any period in the past and future can be designated by a number and made the basis for a calculation, forecast or prediction. If the cards in the card index of norms are designated by numbers, then how can one establish an unambiguous correspondence between numbers and norms. The direction of time is easy connect with the concepts of past and future, but what could be the direction of the norms? Such reference points as good and evil have a different generalized semantic coloring than the past and future. The dynamics of the object are easily compared with the direction from the past to the future, but can we talk about the dynamics of the subject from evil to good? In any case, the empirical facts do not demonstrate anything like that. As for experience, it is easy to imagine its scalar growth, but what its direction could be expressed in remains unclear. All the previous reasoning related to the concept of experience and norms can be repeated in relation to the concept of situations. A situation is a form of compatibility of events. A situation can also be defined as a condition for the acquisition and recording of experience. Only in situations does a person or a subject acquire experience. In the end, situations turn into units of memory, but by what principle they are stored there, no one knows yet. By time? Alphabetically? By association? By analogy? By mutual references?

And yet, one cannot escape the thought that experience, norms, and situations are important for the personality, and that these are useful categories for studying human behavior. Without “situations,” the personality could not learn and gain experience. In the end, norms are formed for situations, and not just like that. A norm is a subjective law of a situation. These are the boundaries of subjective optimality. Experience is a set of generalized norms. To understand a norm only as an ethical restriction, proposed or imposed by society, is at least not necessary. A physical law is also a norm. A norm is an element of ordered behavior.

A law is a “rule of the game” of the objective world, a norm is a rule of the game of the subjective world. The norm is a parameter of the technology of behavior in a specific situation.

But situations change. And even a small, almost imperceptible change in the situation, can significantly change the corresponding norm. The norm is always the norm of reaction and behavior. But at the level of socionic generalization, it is impossible to contrast reaction and behavior - at this level, these categories are identified, become indistinguishable. Reaction is a response to a situation. This is a change of the parameters of the subjective state in response to a change in the parameters of the environment. The environment can also be understood as a source or generator of situations.

Considering socionic concepts, we can distinguish between the object and subject components of the environment. Both components of the environment are objective, but the first is associated with the logical, and the second - with the ethical attitude to the environment. One of the general scientific concepts of objectivity comes down to the independence of the existence of an object in general, and particularly the environment from the subject. But what about the uncertainty principle?

One of its formulations, or rather, consequences, states that, by entering any contact with an object or environment, the subject changes them. That is, even the presence of the subject next to the object should change something. But what is the measure here? Nearby - how much, at what distance? And if we change, then what exactly? Are we not generalizing the uncertainty principle too much? Let us return to its original formulation, which states that it is impossible to simultaneously measure the coordinate of an elementary particle and its energy.

This situation relates to the logical definitions of concepts. What is the coordinate of a particle? After all, if a particle has dimensions (such a concept also needs clarification), then it occupies some part of the space in which it can be detected. To what point of this space should the coordinates of the entire particle be assigned, if, from a mathematical point of view, there are infinitely many points in this section of space? Therefore, the concept of the coordinate of a particle turns out to be a conditional concept. And if we indicate a point coordinate, then we thereby indicate an infinitely small part of the particle, then in the infinitely small part of the particle there will be an infinitely small amount of its energy. But the larger part of the particle we cover to estimate the energy of the particle, the more uncertain its position becomes. If the theorist concludes that this is not a corpuscle of limited dimensions, but a wave formation, which in the limit extends to the entire space of its existence, then it is necessary to somehow determine its position in a special way. The fact that a particle may turn out to be infinite does not mean at all that it will have infinite energy.

Mathematically, this is well understood by analogy with infinite curves whose area has a finite value. For example, the famous Gauss curve.  The same can be said about some infinite (here it would be more accurate to speak not of infinity, but of infinity) surfaces, the volume of which is limited.  One such surface can be obtained by rotating the Gauss curve around its axis of symmetry. From the previous discussions, it seems to follow that the uncertainty principle owes its formulation to imprecise definitions.

However, let us continue the discussion of this famous and, apparently, paired doxal principle. Let us consider a specific situation of measuring temperature with a thermometer. A simple analysis shows that the thermometer shows not the temperature of the object, but its own. And its readings are close to the truth, that is, they correspond to the temperature of the object, only if the mass of the thermometer is incommensurably smaller than the mass of the controlled object. Thus, if we measure the temperature of water in a thimble, the distortion may be very large. And it is generally impossible to measure the temperature of a drop in this way. Isn't the anthropic principle an illusion? After all, it is quite possible to believe that the world constants are tuned to the presence of man not due to the existence of an a priori "anthropic principle", but because man was formed in the process of evolution in the field of action of these constants, tuned in to these constants and began to correspond to them. Therefore, it is not clear why there should be any surprise that, at least some world constants, in a sense, are tuned to man. However, the fact is that some deviations of world constants from existing values ​​would be incompatible with the emergence in the world of not only reason, but also life, as we know it.

To begin with, I would not rush to introduce and evaluate the spatial characteristics of mental functions. I would like to first understand their systemic connection. The idea that all functions are interconnected is quite dialectical. In fact, this is the meaning of systemicity and, in particular, integrity. There is a way to theoretically express such a connection. For this, one can imagine that all the others are represented in each function. And, thus, one can, for example, talk about representation of the PPF (Base) in the Creative or Role, etc. This makes it possible to introduce the concept of the same dimensionality of all functions, which in this case will be equal to 8.

But is there any point in introducing spatial representations into the concept of a mental function if there is no certainty with the mental space?

Now we can ask the question, why do they talk about different intensities of work of mental functions in socionics? One of the preliminary answers could be that this is simply incorrect. All functions are loaded approximately equally, but this, for example, may not happen simultaneously - by analogy with flashing lights on the operator's console. In the end, they all work to create the final mental product. Another thing is that the work of each of the functions can be perceived differently. Let us also not forget that functions that differ in vertibility work in parallel, as follows from model "A", and not sequentially, as presented in model "G" (V.V. Gulenko) or "E" (V.D. Ermak).

The above review of various approaches to understanding model "A", as well as its hypothetical generalizations, shows that socionics are discovering more and more new sides in this model and are trying to reconcile it with their own practical experience and methodological complexes. Perhaps, not everything that the authors propose will pass the test of practice, but the very fact that scientific research continues indicates, on the one hand, that not all the problems of socionic modeling of the psyche have been solved, and on the other hand, it instills hope that sooner or later they will be solved. However, socionics should be prepared for the fact that there may be interpretations of Model A that differ to some extent from those currently available, which will only expand and deepen our understanding of the structure and functioning of the psyche. There is also a problem in connection with the concept of receiving and issuing information for each of the generalized mental functions. In some socionic publications, the functioning of the model is described as if information is transmitted linearly from one function to another, and thus, some functions work on receiving, and others on issuing. However, it follows directly from Model A that all functions receive and issue information. Since blocks can also be considered as functions of the next level of generalization, the question of receiving and issuing information applies to them as well. However, there is not enough empirical material to confidently assume how this process occurs. And since each pair of blocks forms a ring, they also need to be considered as even more generalized functions, and the question of receiving and transmitting information here also needs to be resolved.

Transmission and reception of information within a psychic structure can be understood in the sense that information generated in one part of the psyche is transmitted to another part with the help of certain material carriers, which becomes a consumer of this information and based on it, in accordance with its capabilities, generates some new information. Does any information received by the receiving block, ring or function return after processing to the sender? This is a problem that needs to be studied experimentally.

In connection with the formulated problem, Aushra concluded that "the mental ring can be called accepting, but this is true only in relation to the perceived information on the basis of which the vital ring of the dual operates." This partially sheds light on the exchange of information at all levels of functional generalization. That is, information always returns, but not necessarily directly, and the delay time can be as long as desired. In the end, human society is based not only on the direct exchange of information in real time, but also on the delayed communication of generations and individuals.

In the information metabolism of functions, blocks and rings, there seems to be both parallelism and sequence, but experimental research is needed to clarify their features.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MODEL T

All the models of the psyche considered above, including model "A", are speculative in nature, and therefore require experimental verification. The above-mentioned model “T” deserves special attention from the point of view of substantiating model “A” and its verification, since it is formulated in psychophysiological terms that allow direct instrumental measurement. The author of model

“T” V.L. Talanov believes that model “T” is fully verified in a strictly controlled psychophysiological experiment, and this can be understood in such a way that, with an appropriate choice of terms, verification of model “T” can be transferred to verification of model “A”.

Thus, if there is a way to equivalently transform model “T” into model “A”, this means that verification of model “T” is simultaneously verification of model “A”.

Let’s try to outline an algorithm for such a transformation.

In model “T”, if I understand it correctly, each function is represented as having two inputs, one of which is associated with excitation, and the other with inhibition. In this case, each of these inputs works both to receive a signal and to transmit it. Let's take a closer look at the "T" (Ki) model, that is, ILE:

According to this formula-model, the intuitive function Ki is excited only by a strong signal that becomes effective only in tense situations and requires large tasks, a large scope. This is exactly how Aushra describes the behavior of ILE in extreme situations and its general attitude to solving global problems.

And, on the contrary, in stable or routine situations, when the "intuitive differential" approaches zero, this function slows down, and its carrier switches to the "calm contemplation" mode in anticipation of new intuitive loads.

The first function of any extrovert works in a similar mode, being excited when a high or strong signal is received through the information aspect of its filling.

Recall that when constructing model "A", Aushra proceeded from the fact that the functions of the mental and vital rings work synchronously. This can be understood as follows: functions with the same aspects of different vertency represent a single function, the mental and vital part of which are only its different inputs. Is it possible to interpret this situation so that the mental channel of the function ensures the excitation of the function, and the vital one - its inhibition? It is possible that in this case it will be necessary to appropriately change the terminology and clarify the concepts behind it.

According to model "A", an extrovert in the Base function actively seeks high loads, since in this case its tone is in harmony with the situation. But in physiological terminology, this means that the function is excited, that is, enters the working state when a strong signal appears. In addition, it is easy to understand that the signal coming through the mental function is the switching signal, or, in accordance with physiological terminology, the exciting one.

It is possible that significant conceptual clarifications are needed here.

Complementary to Base is the Ignoring function. Can it be understood as an inhibition channel? This is a passive function; it only imperatively ensures the implementation of Base programs.

And if something can be stopped or slowed down here, it is Ignoring. Now we can already make a general hypothetical conclusion that the mental part of each paired function is the channel of its excitation, and the vital part is the channel of its inhibition.

The construction of algorithms for converting model’s "A" and "T" into each other would become a full-fledged means of in-depth understanding of each of them. Of course, a psychophysiological model is necessary, but it is not enough since people need psychological tools in their practical activities.

------------

Conclusions for the fourth chapter

1. Due to the high level of abstraction, model "A", like mathematical formulas, allows for various meaningful interpretations. Theorists from socionics have proposed various schemes aimed at clarifying the understanding of model "A". It is possible that each of these proposals reflects a certain cost the reality.

2. The semantic fields of the functions of model "A" have been clarified.

3. The understanding of model "A" as a set of sixteen functional blocks ready for immediate contact with the corresponding situations in the environment has been proposed and substantiated.

4. An expanded model of TIM has been proposed and substantiated, resulting from the linear arrangement of blocks of model "A" and their regrouping.

5. The understanding of model "A" as a set of functions having mutual representations in each other, which is equivalent to a systemic connection between them, has been proposed and substantiated. An example of mutual representation of body systems is given as a physiological analogue.

6. The problem of experimental verification of model "A" and the need to construct an algorithm for the transition from psychophysiological models to psychological ones and back are considered.

Churyumov Chapter 5

The problem of existence, uniqueness, and diversity within TIM

--

THE PROBLEM OF THE EXISTENCE OF TIM

Does the socionic type really exist?  To answer the question, we must first answer the questions of what is “real” and what is “existence”. Different philosophical systems answer this question differently. We offer the following answer, aimed not at philosophers, but at scientists. One of the meanings of the word "real" is a synonym for "objective". In this sense, both words indicate something that exists independently of the subjective certainty of the observer. Representatives of various philosophical schools can point out several defects in such a statement, but this will depend on the definitions they use. Nevertheless, we will use the words in question in this sense. So, we will speak of real existence if the object behind the word denoting it can be observed and used for practical purposes.

The concept of "existence" is much more complex. There are philosophical schools that believe that the physical world is an illusion, and they provide convincing arguments in favor of this. In this text we will assume that the physical world really exists, that is, it is in "engagement" with the subject, so that the subject-actor cannot ignore it, is forced to reckon with it and adapt to it.

It is easy to recognize as existing objects perceived by the senses or recorded by devices that are an extension and amplifiers of the human sensory system. However, problems arise with those objects that are not recorded by existing devices. These include socionic types. It is easiest to assume that socionic types are not material, but informational objects. Then we can talk about the existence of a type if there is a program of typical behavior recorded in the psyche. Existential judgments, or judgments about the existence of an object, along with attributive and relative judgments, represent an important class of logical judgments that establish the primary qualification of an object as existing or not existing. Without such qualification, all further logical procedures associated with the object in question lose all meaning.

Does TIM, the original object of socionics, exist, and what meaning is attached to the concept of its existence? Is TIM a natural object that can be observed in one way or another in natural conditions or in experimental conditions? Or is it some kind of artificial formation or device that is introduced for the convenience of describing some features of a more complex object, such as, for example, a person or his psyche? Or, the question can be put this way, is it some kind of virtual phenomenon, accessible to formal recording under some special conditions, outside of which TIM is not observed? Questions of this kind should not be considered idle, since the concept of TIM is still not generally accepted in science, has not been included in encyclopedic reference books and dictionaries, and, moreover, it is not self-evident.

Currently, in experimental personality psychology, categories are used that are aimed at describing various parameters of the human psyche and have a rather complex multi-level structure, which is a combination of concepts obtained in a rather complex way with the help of methods that have received wide recognition in psychology. Such categories include, for example, the so-called factors, related to different levels and accordingly designated as factors of the first, second and third order (it goes without saying that the formation of factors of a higher order is also possible). Thus, one of the first-order factors SPIRITUAL ORGANIZATION is defined as a combination of two scales from the MMPI and four scales from the Cattell questionnaire.

The factor is a generalized name for a group of scales and is introduced for an economical description of the individual psychological characteristics of a person.

The semantic content of the factor is revealed through the scales from which it is formed, and this content can be clarified by moving on to an analysis of the structure of the scales at the question level.

What can be said about the reality and existence of objects presumably behind such categories?  To answer this question, let us first generalize the concept of a factor somewhat and introduce the concept of a zero-order factor, which is a really observable feature, trait, attribute, element of behavior, or reaction of a specific person. This could include eye color, lip shape, height, speech rate, gestures, postures, and the characteristic time of decision-making, and everything, everything, everything that can be measured and described by direct observation. Then, first-order factors could include those directly unobservable and unmeasurable features of the human psyche, such as determination, will, kindness, openness, learning ability, insight, suspiciousness, etc., that statistically correlate with certain zero-order factors and can be identified using them and with the help of special procedures, which include psychological tests. Then, we can combine first-order factors into well-interpretable groups, which, of course, requires sufficient ingenuity, and the integral effect associated with these groups can be considered as second-order factors. And this process can be continued until we get a small number of categories that make it possible to economically explain various aspects of human behavior. Such an assembly of factors resembles the creation of toy models from the parts of a children's construction set - from the same parts we can create a large number of dissimilar models, and, in addition, among them there may be models that do not correspond to real existing objects, although, of course, some of the latter can be relatively easily interpreted by imagining a suitable thing, albeit non-existent, but which could well be made and used for the purpose that follows from its design.

Still, such an analogy is not complete, and we can assume that unlike a mechanical constructor, any combination of lower-order factors always forms a factor of the next level, and it can be interpreted in one way or another within the framework of an ad hoc (on occasion) synthesized theory. Thus, there can be various psychological theories, the number of which is determined by the combinatorial potential of the set of initial factors.

Apparently, the above reasoning can serve as one of the explanations of the fact that there are quite a few psychological theories from different sides and in different ways explaining the features of the human psyche. The factors themselves represent, to varying degrees, generalized characteristics of individual aspects of human behavior. Thus, the existence of factors of higher orders can be reduced to directly observable primary factors of zero order, and their existence, by virtue of obviousness, does not require special justification.

However, in the case of a living organism, particularly a human being, zero-order factors can be considered as a trace, projection or relatively stable "sediment" of higher-order factors that act in the organism. If we take two such factors as a square chin and stubbornness, then different opinions are possible regarding the causal relationship between them. It can be assumed that it is stubbornness with its accompanying physiological processes that leads to the formation of such a physiognomic trait. But a directly opposite point of view is also possible, according to which it can be argued that it is the presence of a square chin that is an element that includes the physiological mechanisms on which stubbornness depends. At least in psychology, it is known that if a person is happy, he smiles, but the opposite is also possible: it is enough to portray a sincere smile and you will become happy. So, both points of view have empirical confirmation. But a third point of view is also possible, according to which both stubbornness and a square chin are two forms of unfolding some factor, standing behind these two phenomena. The answer here does not need to be looked for far - such a factor may be a very specific gene. The ancient Greek philosopher Prodicus said: "I see a horse, but I do not see horseness." Medieval scholastics continued this theme in disputes about the reality of the individual and the general.

Perhaps Prodicus and the scholastics would have changed their minds if they knew genetics and socionics. Genetics shows that the genome of all horses has common structural elements that provide the form of a horse, and socionics refers to extroverted and introverted forms of objects that are equally real but are only represented differently in the physical world. In the introverted form of an object, one can identify fragments that provide a frame structure common to all objects of one class.

Similarly, one can talk about the existence of frame programs of behavior that set the most general parameters of human actions. One can identify many such programs. However, many of them, already proposed and used in psychology, are fragmentary or redundant. This is explained by the fact that they do not satisfy the fundamental methodological requirements of completeness, consistency, independence, necessity, sufficiency, and often several others. It turns out that such random combinations of generalized behavioral algorithms, upon closer examination, do not satisfy several well-known logical requirements that are imposed, for example, on definitions, divisions of concepts into classes, judgments, and inferences. This is exactly what we observe in such famous psychological brands as the set of factors of Cattell, MMPI or accentuations identified by Leonhard.

And even such an ancient deductive system of psychology as astrology did not avoid several methodological errors. However, this is one of the reasons for its rejection by science. And, strange as it may seem, many scientists make methodological errors in their reasoning and theoretical constructions, being deeply convinced of their rightness. Why go far when there are many known attempts to prove Euclid's postulate on parallel lines, considering it a theorem. This was done by very disciplined mathematical minds, and yet it turned out that their constructions contained very subtle logical errors. What can we say about non-mathematicians!

Summing up the previous reasoning, we can say that THE SOCIONIC TYPE REALLY EXISTS AS A COMBINATION OF VERY CERTAIN FRAME PROGRAMS OF BEHAVIOR, RECORDED IN MENTAL AND PHYSIOLOGICAL MEDIA. By frame program we mean here generalized and extremely generalized restrictions within which specific behavior is formed.

Socionics is a systematic and coherent theory based on observable data. The structural-phenomenological approach, which can be used as the basis for theoretical constructions of socionics, allows to classify and accurately describe some generalized processes occurring in connection with the human personality. TIM is not a conceptual fiction, a mysterious entity, or a theoretical artifact - it is a structural-phenomenological object that can be discovered because of processing empirical observations. It is completely wrong to consider Jung's typological discoveries as some kind of "conceptual constructions", as, for example, E. Berne does. Their theoretical quality is no worse than E. Berne's transactional analysis, although they are presented in a scientific-philosophical manner, which was still widespread at the beginning of the twentieth century. However, by their nature, these are acceptable generalizations of clinical experience, of which Jung had plenty. All that is necessary here is to present his results in phenomenological language, as, for example, E. Berne does. As for E. Berne himself, despite the high efficiency of the theoretical scheme he developed, he can also be presented with a methodological reproach related to the lack of substantiation of the completeness of the set of personal positions presented in his methodology. The empirical obviousness of this set should not mislead us. Returning to the problem of the existence of TIM, we can say that the latter is one of the possible psychological factors, since it can be assembled from a set of differential features, and thus, its reality and existence are determined by the reality and existence of individual differential features and their sets.

The problem of the existence of TIM can also be approached from another, formal, side. The existence of TIM itself is the initial hypothesis of socionics, and the recognition or non-recognition of such existence determines whether socionics has its own subject of study and is directly related to its scientific status.

Since the hypothesis of the existence of TIM has been tested in practice in various groups, clubs and in solving applied social problems, the existence of TIM should be recognized as a fact. This is recognized as such a fact by those who professionally work with this object.

From a formal theoretical point of view, TIM is postulated by a set of axioms, the truth of which is intuitively seen. Such axioms include:

1) The presence of generalized information aspects Se, Si, Ne, Ni, Fe, Fi, Te, Ti.

2) The presence of generalized psychological functions, called socionic in the framework of socionics and observed in the work of the human psyche.

3) The connection of the information aspect with the work of the mental function.

4) The polarity of generalized information aspects observed and established directly when these aspects are identified.

5) The absence of a smooth transition between the poles marked by information aspects.

This does not exhaust all the axioms. Only those necessary for solving the problem are given here.

Knowing the semantics of information aspects, they can be easily organized using the abandonment and opposition. Contrasting aspects Se, Ne, Fe, Te with aspects Si, Ni, Fi, Ti, we obtain the axis of EXTRAVERSION — INTROVERSION. Contrasting aspects Se, Ne, Si, Ni with aspects Fe. Fi, Te, Ti, we obtain the axis of IRRATIONALITY — RATIONALITY. Contrasting aspects Se, Si, with aspects Ne, Ni, we obtain the axis of SENSORICS — INTUITION. Contrasting aspects Fe, Fi with aspects Te, Ti, we obtain the axis of EMOTIONING — THINKING. Attributing the properties of the psyche of a real person to the corresponding poles leads to the establishment of TIM.

Unambiguity is achieved here only if axiom 5 is fulfilled.

That is, if the transition from one pole to another is made by a jump, if there is no gradual transition between the poles, there are no gradations. It is easy to object here, pointing to the possibility or actual presence of different degrees of extroversion, rationality, sensory, logicality, etc. But the intensity of the quality of a pole does not at all relate to qualities intermediate between the poles. Intermediate qualities should be represented by linear combinations of the qualities of the poles like 3A + B, etc., and have, at least possibly, special names. In the space of the original TIM model, this is not envisaged, and a discrete transition is assumed, a jump from one arrangement of the poles in the model to the opposite. Such a jump can be compared with the quantum transition of an electron from one orbit to another, and it is possible that such an analogy has a real basis if it turns out that the substrate of the psyche is some energy field capable of quantization, and its quantum states correspond to some mental properties, albeit very generalized ones. At the very least, the presence in the human body of energy meridians, with which specific mental and psychological semantics are reasonably associated, is a sufficient basis for the hypothesis expressed above. This problem was partially discussed in the chapter devoted to the hypothetical substrate of the psyche. As for the observed spread of quality intensities, it relates to some other scale being superimposed on the socionic scale, for example, the scale of temperament, erudition, profession or some other. It can be said that from the point of view of socionics, one INTUITIVE-LOGICAL EXTROVERT is no different from another, since it is a type, but a real person of this type, as a rule, is very different from another real person, only these differences are determined by other scales, based on which other typologies are built. Type and character should not be mixed up since these are different realities.

THE PROBLEM OF UNIQUENESS OF TYPE

Can a specific person have several TIMs, and not only simultaneously, but, for example, changing depending on circumstances, situations or at the will of the person himself? The answer to this question depends largely on the definitions. In socionics, TIM is understood as the integral adaptation of the psyche to the perception, selection, and processing of generalized information flows. However, in a broader sense, it seems that we should talk about the perception, selection and processing of MEI complexes, integrated combinations of various forms of manifestation of matter, energy, and information. As a result, secondary entities arise that are qualitatively different from each other and determine the phenomenological basis of the human habitat, which includes not only the physical world, but also the social and individual world. As a result of the total phylogenetic adaptation of the psyche of a specific person to the conditions of existence, each generalized mental function is associated with or is adapted to the processing of one information aspect, and this, apparently, is a consequence of generalized thermodynamic laws, prescribing the minimization of energy costs and energy-consuming configurations. If we exclude a small percentage of special cases, then we can say that the vast majority of people, as a result of interaction with the circumstances of their lives, develop some one type of generalized adaptation, used by them whenever the environment forces them to do so. Moreover, such types could have become genetically fixed in the process of human evolution.

Here it is necessary to distinguish the general form of adaptive reactions from psychological means used by a specific person and which can be very diverse. A person, depending on the situation, can use different types of adjustments or psychological defenses, but all of them, as socionic experience shows, will be within the framework of a single generalized adaptive form, which is precisely the TIM of a given person.

Since TIM is realized on the structure of generalized psychological functions, which have become the subject of socionics and are called socionic, then at least two options for the coexistence of different TIMs could be identified: the presence of duplicate functional configurations filled with theoretical interest and could be realized in reality, at least in a pathological version, but at present there are no experimental data on this issue.

The problem of the uniqueness of TIM is directly related to the problem of the possibility of changing TIM because of specific pressure of life circumstances or targeted training.  One can raise the question of the possibility of convincingly imitating behavior that corresponds to a different TIM than a given person has. This could be done, for example, by artists or other professionals to create a stage image or psychological adjustment. The famous expert in training space crews Bogdashevsky, as an experiment, offered famous Russian actors to play socionic types, but it turned out that an actor, even the most talented, is not capable of fully imitating more than 8 types. Everyone who remembers the remarkable Russian actor Vitsin can understand that he could not play, for example, the great commander G.K. Zhukov, who was so brilliantly played by the outstanding Russian actor Ulyanov. Let us recall that Ulyanov was a carrier of the same TIM as Zhukov, taken by Aushra as a prototype of sensory-logical extroversion.

The stability and the associated uniqueness of TIM in a particular person is well explained by thermodynamic considerations. TIM, regardless of whether it is determined genetically or acquired under the influence of life circumstances, is associated with a certain adaptation and specialization, which, from the point of view of thermodynamics, is related to the minimization of energy costs in the process of human phylogenetic development in their habitat. Since one TIM differs from another by eight Reinin traits and this corresponds to a certain energy barrier, the transition from one TIM to another is energetically unfavorable and has practically not been observed, although, it can be assumed that with the expenditure of a certain amount of energy it can be changed, but for the period of transition from one type to another the individual will have to throw off the protective shell of TIM and remain unprotected, lose all available means of effective communication and psychological protection. But, practically no one agrees to this.

A productive analogy here would be to compare the TIM, for example, with the specialization of an athlete in a particular sport. A weightlifter, to achieve Olympic form, must fully concentrate on the training program, and after achieving a record, it would be almost impossible for him to retrain and become a track and field athlete capable of claiming to achieve Olympic records, for example, in the 100 m run.

THE PROBLEM OF DIVERSITY WITHIN THE TIM

The diversity that can be observed within one type, that is, between people belonging to the same type but having different characters, is apparently determined precisely by the fact that a person cannot be described by one psychological scale. Attempts to explain all the features of a person by his socionic model can be designated as a kind of socionic monoideism. This is in the best case. And more extreme categories here could be socionic fanaticism and socionic chauvinism.

At present, there are several attempts to explain the diversity within the type and the difficulties of socionic testing associated with it.

Such attempts include, for example, the opposition of type and character. In this case, type is presented as the basis, the backbone, the skeleton of various manifestations of personality, and character is a superstructure over this basis, reflecting specific details of the functioning of the personality associated with temperament, upbringing, education, special personal circumstances. Thus, two carriers of the same type can have very different characters. The speed of reactions, the degree of persistence, gentleness, kindness, integrity, features of humor, the prevailing mood, the spectrum of mental capabilities, etc. may differ in a wide range, which may lead to similarity of specific manifestations of different types or sufficient difference of identical ones, and this, naturally, leads to difficulties in socionic testing.

The type is masked by character.

Another attempt to explain intra-type differences is the hypothesis of subtypes (V. Gulenko, A. Didenko, and others). This hypothesis assumes the division of the type into two subtypes - rational and irrational - depending on the dominance of the first or second function in the manifestations of the type. True, here we can make a remark that the first and second functions always differ not only in “rationality”, but also in introvert-extrovert, which for some reason the authors of the subtype hypothesis did not focus on. The authors of this idea proceed from the fact that the model may have an energetic and the first or second function predominates, and therefore a socionic subtype arises. However, this does not solve the issue of diversity, since at best it is only transferred inside the subtype. Moreover, the concept of a subtype associated with a socionic model faces the logical difficulty of introducing this classification category as a taxonomic unit.

We should not just talk about a characterological variety of a Socionic type, but about a subtype of information metabolism as a specific process that is described by a holistic model, the quality of which, as such, is not graduated. Therefore, to introduce the concept of a TIM subtype, it would be necessary to build an independent model that allows for its own gradations. Therefore, special evidence is needed that the observed fluctuations in the characterological features of people belonging to a certain TIM have "intra-model" causes. At the present time, such evidence is lacking.

The subtype hypothesis has one advantage and two disadvantages.

The advantage is that the hypothesis records a certain difference in the character of types, although this still does not eliminate the problem of the diversity of manifestations within the type, but only shifts it to another level - to the level of subtypes. And still there remains the problem of testing, which now relates to the subtype.

On the other hand, this hypothesis has a subtle semantic defect: after all, a socionic type is a TIM - a type of information metabolism, and the concept of a subtype is a classification characteristic, widely used in science to record differences on one basis. In other words, the introduction of subtypes is, in fact, the introduction of a new, more detailed classification of types, and, considering all the ensuing consequences, must be accompanied by the introduction of another structural basis for information metabolism, i.e. an expansion of the functional basis of the type, which is equivalent to the introduction of a new model. Thus, here we observe a subtle substitution of logical concepts. But, of course, it is impossible to prohibit the vulgar use of the concept of a subtype. However, this is already a matter of scientific taste. The introduction of a subtype as a sub-TIM is a hidden paradox, since if a type does not function as such, but only as a subtype, i.e. a sub-TIM, then it is no longer a TIM, and, therefore, not a type. The disidentification of a type with itself within the boundaries of the models used ("J" and "A") at the everyday level means nothing more than a mental disorder.

However, the attempt to identify diversity within a type has a real basis: this diversity is directly observable. The search for the causes of this diversity cannot but excite socionics, and, in connection with the attempt to introduce subtypes, it can be assumed that the energy proportion between all functions (and not just between the first and second) within the conservation of TIM can really explain part of the intra-type diversity. In other words, the behavior of a carrier of a certain type with an enhanced Base will differ from the behavior of a carrier of the same type, but, say, with an enhanced Creative. But is it permissible to evaluate this as a subtype? After all, if we assume that the activity or manifestation of any function from one carrier of TIM to another can vary within wide limits, then starting from what difference in this indicator can we talk about a subtype? However, all this is subject to deep experimental verification. Theoretically, it is even difficult to formulate what, in fact, the strengthening of some generalized function means. On the other hand, it is practically not difficult to observe significant differences in the behavior of people of the same type, when one of them, for example, is better educated or brought up differently. But does this relate to the strengthening of some generalized function? After all, they have the same type! It is also possible that the idea of ​​​​a subtype appears because of the imperfection of testing procedures. It is also possible that the expert's observation of the subtype is nothing more than an illusion that arises because of superimposing other mental factors on the type. At the XXII International Socionics Conference, Gulenko in his report "The Theory of Subtypes: DCNH System" (dominance, creativity, normativity, harmonization) uses a completely different idea of ​​​​subtypes. He superimposes one typology on another and considers the types of this other typology as subtypes of the first typology. In this case one can propose as many subtype systems as there are different typologies you want to use. Here, the concept of a subtype, losing its genetic connection with the basic typology, acquires a situational connotation, when anyone can consider any set of features that they can find in a person as subtypes.

As another source of intratype heterogeneity, one can also propose the hypothesis of socionic accentuations. The author of this concept proceeds from the observed fact that a socionic type can be “colored” by manifestations of any other type, and not just be softer or harder, as it happens in the case of accepting the theory of subtypes.

We will call a socionic accentuation a case when within the framework of a certain socionic type, sometimes masking, sometimes emphasizing, but generally deforming it, manifestations of another type are demonstrated. The appearance of such “phantom” effects was noted by many socionics. Earlier than others and more often than others, the “phantom” of the dual was noted. Ausra was the first to talk about this in her lectures on socionics. She associated this with the process of self-dualization, occurring under certain special conditions in the absence of a dual, when it is necessary to perform work that is usually expected from a dual, the functions of the vital ring are activated. Later, other phantoms began to be encountered during testing. For example, there were cases when some of the external manifestations, primarily physiognomic, corresponded to the Mirror, Activator, Quasi-identical, Related, Superego and even Conflictor. Here we can talk, for example, about the accentuation of SEI or ESI, when ILE becomes like his Conflictor, etc. There were pairs of ILE and ESI, similar in the ferocity of their facial expressions, in the rigidity of their line. However, upon further examination it turned out that in ILE this related to mental confidence in the correctness of his ideas, in the correctness of his position, and in ESI it related to subjective self-confidence, supported by the ability to oppose his partner with unbending severity. One can also note the pairs IEE - LSI, physiognomically similar in their specially designed moustaches ("brush moustache") and witty-sarcastic facial expression. Later it turned out that IEE's whisker design tends to the shape of a convex brush, while LSI's tends to the shape of a straight brush.

The conflict in this pair often develops in the style of witty sparring, but the nature of their wit is different. In LSI, wit has the character of subtle logical constructions, while in IEE it is a firework of unexpected comparisons, etc.  In pairs LSE - IEI, one can often observe a similarity in neatness and everyday tidiness in clothes, but the reasons for this are different for each type: LSE feels the quality of the goods, "observes" the form, and IEI subconsciously is set to please his gloomy dual.

Generalization of the above observations leads to the idea that phantom accentuations of the socionic type are possible for all types of relationships. To substantiate such a hypothesis, an appropriate model is needed. The appearance of phantom accentuations within a quadra is easiest to explain. Within a quadra, identical or mirror-symmetrical functions of model "A" are used. Each function, working in the corresponding energy mode, makes its contribution to the energy aura of the type, which is reflected in the corresponding elements of appearance. So, with constant activation conditions of any function, there is an opportunity to change its energy with corresponding consequences.

Let us recall the effect of striking similarity of spouses who have lived a long life together or the "similarity" of dogs and cats to their owners.

The concept of socionic accentuation increases the possibilities of diversity, but still does not exhaust it. The assumption of socionic accentuations does not require the introduction of an additional taxonomic unit and can be explained by strengthening the intra-model radical of the corresponding TIM. Such strengthening can occur under the influence of external and internal causes. These may include upbringing, self-dualization, targeted training, the need for secondary adaptation to changed circumstances.

An interesting hypothesis that offers its contribution to explaining the diversity within a TIM is used in V.D. Ermak’s communicative models. The author proceeds from the fact that the type is covered by a mask of conditioned reflexes that are not characteristic of this type, developed in a certain social environment, and based on which it can be mistakenly attributed to another type. Here, too, the problem of logical qualification of concepts arises. If we are talking about a model here, then which one? If this is a model like the socionic one, but at the same time differing from the main TIM, then it is necessary to prove that in the human psyche, along with the structure of socionic functions, an alternative structure arises that completely duplicates or replaces the main socionic structure.

Otherwise, the term "model" is either redundant or has semantics that do not coincide with the semantics of the socionic model. Here, for example, we could talk about a mask, but this concept also requires theoretical justification. 

It seems that the problem of the complexity of human character cannot be solved within the framework of any one typology. However, it is interesting to consider the possibilities of socionics from this point of view. Without claiming categorical and final conclusions, let us consider the hypothesis of COMPLETENESS OF SOCIONIC REPRESENTATION OF HUMAN CHARACTER. Socionics, as was shown in the work "Type and Character", in its semantic completeness is comparable with three well-known and universal typologies such as MMPI, Leonhard's typology of accentuations and Lichko's typology. The logical sum of their semantic fields coincides with the semantic field of socionics. On the other hand, if we compare the diagnostic capabilities of MMPI and Cattell's questionnaire, then, given the universality of both methods and the nature of the results obtained in them, we can say that the effectiveness of these methods is approximately the same. From this we can conclude that the semantic fields of both methods are at least close, which is, of course, not surprising, since both methods are focused on a wide range of applications and are performed by high-class professional psychologists. It also follows from this that the semantic field of socionics is at least no smaller, which means that methods no less powerful than Cattell's questionnaire and MMPI can be created on its basis. These conclusions inspire hope that the problem of diversity within TIM can eventually be resolved by the internal capabilities of socionics itself.   Work in this direction continues.

This hypothesis has another equally important basis. Back in 1993,

A.V. Bukalov showed that in socionics the principle of fractality is implemented in various forms, applicable to various structures, in one way or another connected with the basic socionic model "A". Such, for example, is the structure of a small group, well, but, as it turned out after the article of A.V. Bukalov, insufficiently, studied in psychology: the total number of roles in this group is not seven, as it is written in psychology textbooks, but eight, and its structure, "with an accuracy of fractality", corresponds to the structure of model "A". The fractals of model "A" are the socion itself, and the quadras, and the fractal extensions of model "A" into the physical and supramental realm (A.V. Bukalov, V.D. Ermak). The socionic structure of the ethnos (A.V. Bukalov) is also a fractal analogue of the model "A". And even the situational representation of the subjective perception of the operator of the features in the process of diagnosing the TIM fits into a fractal structure, which can look (according to A.V. One of the mental fractals that influence the diversity within TIM is what can be called the typology of psychosomatic accentuation of character (V.K. Torchak). This typological direction originates from Freud, who described three stages of erotic development of personality: oral, anal and genital. Mental fixations at one stage or another in childhood manifest themselves in adulthood as quite specific character traits. For example, anal fixation forms such personality traits as stubbornness, thrift, neatness, as well as fixation on the past. Somewhere by the mid-nineties of the twentieth century, this typology, through the efforts of several psychologists, was brought to eight types, to which, in addition to those mentioned, urethral, ​​cutaneous, visual, olfactory, verbal, and auditory were added. In the presented form, the multitude of psychosomatic character accentuations looks like an eclectic-empirical list, since there is no proof of its completeness. In addition, it includes representative systems from NLP, which makes these typological units unequal in their psychological qualification. Of course, this list needs further theoretical development. However, there is some hint of a psychosomatic fractal and its influence on the diversity within the type.

The psychogeometry of S. Delinger, who managed to make a brand out of a rather simple typology, can also be attributed to the fractal psychological multitude.

At one time, Freud developed the theme of psychological defenses, of which he had eight, but later various psychologists identified about two dozen more defenses, and they can also be represented as a single fractal, the theoretical development of which is still awaiting its researchers.

The hypothesis put forward by A.V. Bukalov about the psych informational field, the carrier of information functions and structures, also has a direct relation to the solution of the problem of diversity within the TIM.  According to this hypothesis, all structural phenomena associated with the psyche, society and ethnicity are resonances of a hypothetical field, and therefore, according to its laws, will be like a certain extent. If this hypothesis is proven experimentally, then another promising direction for a meaningful description of the diversity within the TIM will open up, and perhaps then it will be possible to find a common basis for a large number of currently existing typologies.

------------

In conclusion, perhaps, from a practical point of view, there is no sense in reducing all typologies to a common denominator since they are effectively used as working tools in their subject area.  However, it is possible that a unified theory of the psycho-informational field could not only become a common basis for many typologies, but they, in addition to a deeper theoretical justification, could be presented in a new light, and their effectiveness would become higher.

Within the framework of socionics, there is at least one more possibility to describe the diversity within a TIM as a different percentage of radicals of relationships and radicals of types in a type.  It was shown in the chapter on modeling the human psyche, the socionic type can be represented as a set of psychic radicals, which are information-energy instruments ready for contact with the corresponding type of situations. Each such radical can be represented either as a generalized relation or as a typical intention. A typical intention can be defined as an extremely condensed typological reaction. When such an intention is turned on, the personality does not become a carrier of another type but uses the corresponding radical as an instrument of adaptation to the environment. The role of such radicals is especially noticeable in pathological or conditionally pathological cases.

So, if a person's identity mechanism (Ego Block) is weakened, distorted or destroyed, then the task of self-realization for him becomes either difficult or completely impossible. When the dualization mechanism (Super-Id) is destroyed, a person is doomed to loneliness. If the activation mechanism (Mobilizing > Suggestive reverse flow block) is weakened or disabled, then the person will constantly be at a low energy level, which dooms him to reduced productivity. When the mirror mechanisms (Creative >Base reverse flow block) are destroyed, the person is incapable of a realistic and adequate perception of reality, with all the ensuing dramatic consequences.

Defects in the order and control mechanisms make a person inadequate in transmitting social influences, which leads to his inferiority as a social being. The destruction of the business valence (Role > Creative reverse flow block) is expressed in the inability to contact other people on an equal footing.  And the defect of the mirage radical (Ignoring > Mobilizing reverse flow block) leads to slavish dependence on any possible influences, to the internal lack of freedom of the individual. Similar conclusions are possible for all sixteen psychic radicals.

The expression of any psychic radical is individual for each person and varies widely within people of the exact same type.  From complete absence to sizes determined by fractions of 1.0. Thus, a specific "layout" of the fractional value of psychic radicals determines the life effectiveness of an individual with high accuracy.

Let's take, for example, a random individual SLE who happens to have the following levels of psychic radical expressiveness:

Identical (Se Base > Ti Creative) = 0.8,  Duality (Ni Suggestive > Fe Mobilizing) = 0.3,  Activation (Fe Mobilizing > Ni Suggestive)  = 1,  Mirror (Ti Creative > Se Base)  = 0.5,  Beneficiary (Fe Mobilizing > Si Ignoring)  = 1,  Semi-dual (Ni Suggestive > Te Demonstrative)  = 0.2,  Supervisee (Ti Creative> Ne Role)  = 0.9,  Supervisor (Fi PoLR > Se Base) = 1,  Business (Ne Role > Ti Creative) = 0.4,  Mirage (Si Ignoring > Fe Mobilizing) = 0.6,  Quasi-identical (Te Demonstrative > Si Ignoring)  = 0.1,  Conflict (Fi PoLR > Ne Role)  = 0.7,  Super-ego (Ne Role > Fi PoLR)  = 0.5,  Contrary (Si Ignoring> Te Demonstrative)  = 0.1, Kindred (Se Base > Fi PoLR)  = 0.9,  Benefactor (Te Demonstrative > Ni Suggestive)  = 0.7.

What is hidden behind this? This particular SLE (as each is different) has a rather high intention for self-realization (Se Base > Ti Creative = 0.8) but is almost incapable of love (Ni Suggestive > Fe Mobilizing = 0.3), but highly active (Fe Mobilizing > Ni Suggestive = 1.0).  This fragment of the characteristic already sets a specific image of generalized behavior of a robotic type. If we add to this a low level of adequacy of assessment of the proposed circumstances (Ti Creative > Se Base = 0.5), the maximum ability to project oneself onto others (Fe Mobilizing > Si Ignoring = 1.0) and a very low ability of empathy (Ni Suggestive > Te Demonstrative = 0.2), then it will become clear that here a strong accusatory position is combined with a lack of sympathy for another. If we now consider that the studied creature with high intensity monitors objects and circumstances to intervene (Ti Creative > Ne Role = 0.9), but at the same time almost slavishly depends on another authority (Fi PoLR > Se Base = 1.0), then it will become clear that this is a tough and uncompromising executor of someone else’s will.

Usually this is the will of a superior or a close person (wife, daughter, etc.). Another possible option is a tyrant-dictator- husband. In addition, such a person has a very limited outlook (Te Demonstrative > Si Ignoring = 0.1), is like a dog ready to break loose from the chain at any moment (Fi PoLR > Ne Role = 0.7), but at the same time is almost incapable of independently developing goals (Si Ignoring > Te Demonstrative =0.1), and does not fully possess diplomatic skills (Ne Role > Fi PoLR =0.5). It remains to add to what has been said that he has sufficient artistic abilities (Se Base > Fi PoLR = 0.9) and a lot of claims (Te Demonstrative > Ni Suggestive = 0.7).

However, we are not interested in the specific subject we have outlined here, but in the possibility of sufficiently detailing the character, considering the proportional assessment of the psychic radicals included in the personality structure. Of course, here we can also talk about the personality profile expressed in socionic radicals.

To explain the typological blurriness, the concept of a mask is used in the works of I. Kalinauskas and T. Prokofieva. E. Krivosheev also talks about this in his book. The concept of a mask also sheds some light on the problem of diversity within a type, but it is easy to understand that it does not cover this topic completely, since the real life of an individual cannot be reduced only to masking the process of self-realization. This topic is discussed in more detail in the chapter "Socionics and Psychology".

Conclusions on the fifth chapter

1. The existence of TIM is the initial hypothesis of socionics, and the recognition or non-recognition of such existence determines the presence of socionics’ own subject of research and is directly related to its scientific status.

2. A SOCIONIC TYPE REALLY EXISTS AS A COMBINATION OF QUITE CERTAIN FRAME PROGRAMS OF BEHAVIOR, RECORDED IN MENTAL AND PHYSIOLOGICAL MEDIA.

3. Returning to the problem of the existence of TIM, it can be said that the latter is one of the possible psychological factors, since it can be assembled from a set of differential features, and thus, its reality and existence are determined by the reality and existence of individual differential features and their sets.

4. From a formal theoretical point of view, TIM, and therefore its existence, is postulated by a set of axioms, the truth of which is seen intuitively or accepted for practical reasons.

5. Since the hypothesis of the existence of TIM has been tested in practice in various groups, clubs and in solving applied social problems, the existence of TIM must be recognized as a fact. This is recognized as such a fact by those who professionally work with this object.

6. As a result of the total phylogenetic adaptation of the psyche of a specific person to the conditions of existence, each mental function is associated or is adapted to the processing of one information aspect, and this ensures the uniqueness of TIM in an individual person, but the structure of the psyche allows for additional adaptation to changing conditions of existence, as a result of which adaptive accentuations may appear, which, due to the peripheral position in the model, still do not replace the main type, but only impose an additional shade on it.

7. The diversity within TIM can be explained by the imposition of other typological scales on the socionic type, but it is of interest to explain the diversity within the type by the variable fractalization of the primary information essence.
