Chapter 6 The Problem of Differentiating Features in Psychology and Socionics

In psychology, there is a concept of personality traits. In the literature you can find the following definition of this concept. Personality traits are stable, repeating in different situations features of an individual's behavior. These include trans-situational and potential measurability. The term “trans-situational” means that the specified behavioral characteristics of an individual can be observed in a variety of situations, while “potential measurability” is the ability to evaluate a particular behavioral characteristic by its degree of expression, intensity, etc. using methods specially developed and adapted for this purpose.

However, such statements should be treated with caution since they depend on the initial positions of the corresponding scientific schools. For example, in connection with the development of socionics, it was discovered that different authors of various psychological methods fill the concepts of extroversion and introversion with different content, sometimes far from coinciding with that which was put into it by its discoverer. Thus, at present, there are at least four versions of this concept - according to Jung, according to Eysenck, experimental-psychological and socionic. Here we will not go into the analysis of these differences but will only note that the socionic understanding of extroversion is as close as possible to its interpretation by C. G. Jung, however, it has its own semantic overtones since C. G. Jung developed these concepts less than socionics.

In a general scientific sense, personality traits can be considered as features by which one personality can be distinguished from another or to identify elements of the same personality's behavior. This can be done to argue the possibility that a specific action, for example, a crime, was committed by a certain person. If such a feature can be used as a distinguishing or contrasting one, it can be classified as a differentiating feature.

Differentiating features can relate to different levels of personality and individuality functioning. Different sources indicate a different number of such levels. In connection with the specifics of the topic, we can offer a more expanded list of levels. It seems that such levels and areas could be genetic, physiological, archetypal, physical, everyday, stereotypical, mental, interpersonal, professional, ethnic, ideological, spiritual. However, we would like this list to be deductively substantiated rather than empirical.

Genetic: phenotypic traits, energetic features, recessive-dominant.

Physiological: features of the functioning of physiological systems, including the functioning of the nervous system with its balance-imbalance, strength-weakness, excitation and inhibition parameters, mediator system, etc.

Archetypal: primary attitudes related to the most general division of reality. This level defines the reality with which the individual's consciousness deals.

Physical: build, height, plasticity, features of the shape of individual parts of the body: head, face, forehead, eyebrows, eyes, nose, mouth, lips, ears, hair, chin, hands, fingers, timbre, energy, and variations in the volume of the voice, variations in the motor tempo-rhythm, etc.

Cultural-functional: neatness, housekeeping, organization, good manners, attitude to the environment, habits, and stereotypes.

Psychological: temperament, level of accentuation, volitional features, features of attention and memory, self-control, etc.

Personality: politeness, distance, initiative, etc.

Professional: degree of professionalism, presence of professional skills.

Ethnic: behavioral characteristics associated with belonging to a certain ethnic group and culture.

Worldview: presence of beliefs and their nature, presence of prejudices, ideology, consciousness, pragmatism, patriotism, subjectivity, tolerance, etc.

Spiritual: the degree of spiritual maturity and aspiration, enlightenment.

--------------

The author does not insist on the completeness of this list, nor on its theoretical correctness, but gives it as an example of an empirical list with all the shortcomings and contradictions inherent in the empirical approach.

It would be wrong to contrast the two existing directions in psychology in the study of personality by identifying psychological traits that characterize personality and by identifying personality types. Specifying only the type of a specific personality, without specifying its characteristic features, greatly impoverishes and simplifies the idea of ​​the person being diagnosed, making such an idea schematic. On the other hand, a list of characteristic features, if it is sufficiently complete, makes it possible to uniquely identify a person, which, of course, is of primary importance for a specific work, but makes such a list problematic from the point of view of its completeness. In addition, when there is a list of characteristic features, then specifying the type can become a valuable generalization of such a list, helping to create a holistic image of a person. Therefore, both approaches are not only valuable in themselves, but are deeply interconnected.

The point is that any number of traits, including one, can be used as a typological criterion. For example, if we take courage as such a trait, then we can talk about identifying a type of courageous people who may be as different from each other as you like in all other respects, but such information can be effectively used when forming groups or contingents to perform some special tasks. However, this approach can mask the polar nature of such a construct as a trait, because by identifying the type of a courageous person, we thereby explicitly or implicitly identify the type of a timid person.

Here it is useful to pay attention to the fact that the pair “brave-timid” in logic is characterized as contradictory, in contrast to the pair “brave-cowardly”, which belongs to the category of contradictory. The first pair indicates two non-intersecting sets, while between the poles of the second pair there can be any number of intermediate elements. However, both pairs indicate fuzzy sets, and psychology has not yet found ways to work with such sets. In other subject areas, for example, in engineering or law, the problem of fuzzy sets is often solved conventionally, that is, artificially establishing restrictions suitable for solving the problem. However, in psychology, such artificial restrictions look like a capitulation to the need for theoretical development of this topic. For example, one can try to artificially assign 3, 4, 5, 100 gradations of courage by writing appropriate explications or tests if such a practical need arises, but will there be a real essence behind this? At the same time, in this case, there are real psychophysiological processes that provide a mental reaction that can be used as a basis for ensuring courage as a psychological phenomenon - these are real differences in the features of the autonomic nervous system. In any case, a psychological trait is always a pole of a construct consisting of at least two poles. Although it is possible to imagine differentiating constructs consisting of three, four, five or more poles.  If two traits are taken as a typological basis, and, namely, in a polar design, then they generate four types.

The naive-empirical approach to the concept of a personality trait is well reflected in common word usage in various languages. A person can be described as cheerful, but stingy; cautious, but simple; forgetful, but treacherous; liberal, but mean, etc. Such characteristic categories have been developed in the culture of all peoples, and they are quite sufficient to serve the “folk” psychology and familiar everyday situations.

A more developed, semi-theoretical approach can be found in scientific psychology, where, using tests developed on one or another theoretical basis, they try to determine such parameters of a person as businesslike attitude (test: "How businesslike are you"), what kind of colleague are you (test: "What kind of colleague are you"), how independent are you (test: "Independence does not hurt anyone"), are you active enough, are you decisive, do you have a talent for conducting business discussions, how well do you navigate in arbitrary situations, do you have "punching power", are you ready for the unexpected, are you inherently objective, do you know how to influence others, what is the level of your aspirations, how docile are you, are you reliable and can you be relied on, are you charming, what is your stress resistance, and are you at risk of nervous breakdown, are you lucky, do you know how to listen to others, how conflict-prone are you, do people around you love you, how organized are you, can you organize and lead people, do you know yourself, do you know how to take risks, are you authoritative, do you have a strong will, etc. Even this small list of those mentioned in psychological literature of tests makes it possible to imagine the empirical randomness of the categories selected to assess a person. The usual criteria for assessing such lists - how complete and mandatory they are and how mutually independent and consistent the categories used in them are - show that the array of currently existing tests is a large but poorly organized set.

In connection with the idea of ​​the mutual dependence or independence of characterization concepts, the problem of identifying basic categories through which all the others could be expressed arises. There is a far from substantiated assumption that, for example, in the Cattell and MMPI systems, such categories are identified and through them all other characteristics of a person can be expressed. This is the basis for recommendations that can be given to a person after examining him with the tests used in these systems.

However, there are also more subtle and disguised criteria for assessing concepts. One of them is the certainty, unambiguity or clarity-fuzziness (in the logical sense) of the concepts used in such lists. If we take, for example, such a psychological quality as will, then its ordinary, everyday, intuitively understandable to native speakers meaning does not withstand critical analysis carried out using scientific methodology.

In this case, it is very quickly discovered that this simple word, as a term, hides several not just different, but even opposite concepts. Thus, we can distinguish between the will aimed at overcoming external obstacles, the will of breakthrough, and the will that makes it possible to stop the internal, subconscious pressure that makes a person a puppet of his own desires and impulses. And often people who can win a tough confrontation with an experienced and strong opponent find themselves helpless not only against drugs, which they have become dependent on, but they cannot even cope with quite “harmless” smoking. One can even assume that such strong-willed, “cool” people cannot, for example, quit smoking, because it is their will that “smokes”, and it cannot cope with itself, since it is equal to itself.

The original approach to the formation of an array of psychological characteristics of a person was used by American psychologists G.V. Allport, H.S. Odbert and R.B. Cattell, who continued the work they started and later became famous.

G.V. Allport, H.S. Odbert carried out work on compiling a dictionary of terms that are usually used to describe a person. They analyzed 18,000 words with a "psychological" connotation available in dictionaries and selected 4,500 words from them that clearly, in their understanding, denoted personality traits and stable behavioral characteristics.

-------

Raymond Cattell

Cattell did further work with this list, identifying synonymous groups in it, and then from each such group he selected a word that, in his opinion, most clearly expressed the main semantic content of such a group, as a result of which he obtained a list of 171 words that cannot yet be considered terms, since they have not undergone full technological processing within the framework of scientific theory. Cattell subjected this list to further processing, which consisted of its assessment by a group of experts, where each indicated the degree of his familiarity with each of these 171 personality characteristics. Having conducted a correlation analysis of the array of assessments obtained because of the experts' work, Cattell identified 36 correlation Pleiades, within which there were highly correlated concepts expressing, as he believed, the same meanings.

These Pleiades also included members with a high negative correlation, such as: silent - talkative, cheerful - sad, trusting - suspicious, etc. Cattell supplemented this array of 36 polar characteristics to 46 pairs, adding special terms taken from the works of other researchers.

And, finally, a technical definition was compiled for each pair. The following can be taken as examples of such definitions.

Flexible. Easily changes his plans, easily restructures, is capable of compromises. He is not surprised, does not become irritable, does not abandon his plans, and does not change his plans if the development of events does not coincide with his expectations.

Rigid. Insists that everything is done the way he is used to doing it, does not change his habits and behavior under pressure from others, gets lost if the usual ways of behavior do not lead to success.

Conscientious. Always honest, knows the rules of behavior well, and always follows them, even if no one is watching him. Never lies or deceives, treats other people with respect.

Shameless. Unscrupulous in the means, does not strive to observe moral principles; when it comes to personal gain, can resort to lies and deception, does not respect the dignity of other people.

We note that even in such scientifically oriented explications, avoid ambiguity. For example, it turns out that conscientiousness coincides with honesty and respect for people, as if a person cannot be honest and not respect people, or, say, consciously commit evil and not follow the rules of behavior.

Later, Cattell concluded that this set of bipolar signs can be "collapsed" to 12-15 factors. Using this circumstance, Cattell constructed a 16-factor "Q" test, that is, a test based on the analysis of responses to specially composed questions. Later, the number of factors was expanded to 19.

The work done by Cattell is a pragmatic attempt to identify "pure" psychological concepts, the effectiveness of which would be high and would not raise doubts. Cattell managed to develop such a method of interpreting a set of factors characterizing a specific person that it can be used to give many practical recommendations that may well prove useful. It is believed that this test has proven itself well, and it has enjoyed and continues to enjoy sufficient popularity.

However, a closer methodological analysis of Cattell's approach to identifying the main psychological categories casts doubt, for example, on the completeness and mandatory nature of the set of factors he obtained. One gets the impression that there could have been more or fewer of them - 12, 16, 19 - and this would not have played a special role in the development of the apparatus for interpreting them. The set of Cattell's factors resembles a good set of carpenter's tools, which includes hammers, saws, drills, chisels, gouges, etc., and which can be supplemented with some other useful tool if necessary. And this is not bad, at least at first glance. Who would object to a set of good tools?

Similar remarks can be made about many other psychological typologies, for example, the MMPI method, in which its ten main categories were a generalization of rich clinical experience, but which are even more down-to-earth empirical in nature than Cattell's factors. All this, however, is in perfect accord with the peculiarities of the American national character, where practical usefulness is put ahead of theoretical "intricacies".

-------------

The same can be said about Virginia Satir's "stances", Everett Shostrom's manipulator types, or Dellinger's "geometric" types. These sets of categories can be said to be practical, aesthetic, and heuristic, but their theoretical justification leaves much to be desired or is completely absent.

For example, S. Delinger believes that she has built a "psychic system", a psychological system, only on the basis that the methodology she developed has been implemented in more than 20 countries, is easily assimilated by the consumer, and leads to easily identifiable practical results. Of course, this is good, but what does all this have to do with theoretical accuracy? Such developments can be attributed to the category of technologies, but, alas, not to the category of science.

In some cases, the completeness of the set of derivative categories can be ensured by a well-chosen polar pair of concepts. For example, in T. Leary's method of diagnosing interpersonal relationships, three polar pairs of categories "dominance-subordination", "friendliness-unfriendliness", "emotionality-analyticity" define eight derivative concepts, which are then used to describe situations arising in intertype relationships.

But even in this method the basic categories do not seem obligatory, although from a pragmatic point of view they seem successful. Of course, there may be such an answer that preferable categories do not exist in principle, but this should still be proven.

Logic has long had a problem of clear and vague concepts. Not only evaluative concepts with a subjective coloring, such as “good” or “beautiful”, are vague, but also qualitative concepts, the denotation of which, that is, the reality behind them, could well be assessed quantitatively, such as “old”, “fat”, “healthy”, “cheerful”. Such words, quite suitable for describing everyday cases and for use in fiction, become non-constructive as soon as they begin to be treated as scientific terms.

According to the degree of certainty, several groups of concepts are distinguished: 1) with a certain content and a sharp registered or unregistered volume ("African countries", "molecule"); 2) with an indefinite content and a sharp registered or unregistered volume ("an experienced teacher at our university", "butterfly"); 2) with an indefinite content and a soft registered or unregistered volume ("a cloudy November morning", "a good transmission"). For example, as regards the indefiniteness of the concept "butterfly", perhaps an entomologist does not have any particular problems here, but for an ordinary person it would be difficult to draw a line between all possible moths and flies, on the one hand, and full-fledged butterflies, on the other.

In professional and scientific practice, where the vagueness of concepts leads not only to errors and misunderstandings but can be of a dramatic and even tragic nature, this logical defect is eliminated by introducing more precise criteria for distinguishing denotates or by special conventions. For example, a person can be considered an adult from the moment he receives a passport, and then two teenagers with an age difference of one day for the same crime will receive very different punishments simply because one has turned sixteen and the other has not.

It should also be considered that pairs of concepts with a high negative correlation can be in a relationship of contrast and contradictoriness. In the first case, the concepts represent polar meanings of a more general category (“white - black”), between which there can be an infinite number of intermediate meanings. In the second case, there are no intermediate values ​​between the poles, but one of the poles can be extremely vague - for example, "white - non-white". In the case of physical objects, certainty can be achieved through measurements and conventions. In the case of psychological categories, their measurability is a difficult problem.

In view of the extreme importance of the problem of differentiating features in psychology, many attempts have been made to solve it, and the results achieved in this direction have been used in practice with varying degrees of effectiveness. Let us consider two such approaches.

------

Osgood’s Semantic differential method

In 1957, Charles E. Osgood developed the concept of semantic differential, designed to measure differences in the understanding of objects, situations, and categories by specific people. This was done with the aim of establishing the subjective and individual attitude of a given person, formed because of his personal practical experience.

For this purpose, the object under study (in verbal or non-verbal form) is proposed to be compared with the value of the scale specified by the polar features. By default, it is assumed that the space between these features is continuous, and the expression of the feature changes monotonically from the zero value, located in the middle between the poles, to one or another pole.

According to Osgood, any object and any concept can be projected onto 3 generalized factor scales: The evaluation factor, the strength factor, and the activity factor.

The scales themselves, being presumably orthogonal, define a three-dimensional factor space. The position of an object in such a space is determined qualitatively (by its correspondence to the scale) and quantitatively (by its distance from the zero value of the factor). Thus, an object of arbitrary nature can be represented by a point in a three-dimensional factor space, which makes it possible to establish the degree of similarity or difference between objects using the procedure of measuring the Pythagorean distance between points representing objects.

This is a beautiful and heuristic idea, and it has not been fully exhausted to this day. However, the weak point here is the assumption of the continuity of the feature space, and most importantly, the subjectivity in the coordinate-semantic positioning of a specific object.

Considering the limitations in the construction of the Osgood space imposed by the subject area of ​​psychology, such a methodological tool can be used to obtain useful results. However, the choice of initial factors itself still does not satisfy the criterion of completeness - at least it has not been proven that three factors are enough to describe the psychological space of a person. In addition, the semantic differential method assumes by default that the selected factors are universal and adequate in relation to an arbitrary subject.

-----

Kelly’s Repertory grid technique

In 1955, George Alexander Kelly developed an individually oriented approach to subjective scaling, in which the determining factors were not imposed by the experimenter from the outside but were extracted from the subjective experience of the individual being studied. The author called this method the repertory grid technique. It is designed to identify an individual system of constructs, or primary categories formed in the human psyche based on personal experience for assessing objects, phenomena, and situations within their environment.

To identify a system of personal constructs, the subject is asked to indicate in his own words, and therefore relying only on his own experience, the difference between objects that are personally significant to him. For this purpose, universal roles are selected that have a specific meaning in the life of each person - father, mother, grandmother, grandfather, son, brother, sister, girlfriend, friend, boss, subordinate, etc. There are twenty-six roles in total, not all of which may be used, and the subject must indicate the existing differences between individual real people from his environment and their various groups by type: how do these two differ from each other at the same time. Processing the obtained results using latent analysis methods allows us to identify the structure of semantic parameters that form the basis of a person's perception of themselves and the world around them.

----------

Differences between Osgood and Kelly approaches.

Both approaches have their positive and negative sides.  In both cases, we are faced with a source of hidden errors.

In Osgood’s semantic differential method, a person inserts an object into a space prepared in advance for this, in general, with evaluation scales alien to the subject.  In this method, it is assumed by default that the subject understands the meaning of the factors selected by the experimenter in the same way as the experimenter, but this is not at all necessary.  The experimenter cannot assert and cannot be sure that the subject understands the categories offered to him in the exact same way as the experimenter. 

In Kelly’s repertory grid technique, the situation is exactly the opposite.  Kelly suggests that a person build a semantic space himself.  The experimenter assumes by default that they understand the constructs of the subject in the same way as the subject. But the experimenter cannot assert and cannot be sure that he understands the categories used by the subject in the exact same way as the subject. 

For the experimenter, depending on the tasks facing him, it may be of interest to know why and how the subject uses his own categories to describe what seems to be the same reality. Perhaps this would help to shed light on the mysteries of subjectivity, but in many cases the experimenter needs or must answer completely different questions, when the subjective world of the subject may remain in the background.

-----------

Let's take this into account and try to use the positive aspects of both methods when solving the problem of differentiating features.

First, let's abandon the understanding of a feature in its linguistic design, since it falls into the category of vague. Second, let's consider that the verbal form of presentation of a feature requires identifying its internal semantic spectrum, that is, determining the qualitative and quantitative gradations existing within it. Thirdly, we will accept that features are objectively realized when contrasting objects or their sets as extensive and intensive differences between them.

We will discuss the last point specifically. Differences can be of an extensive and intensive nature. By an extensive representation of differences, we will understand directly registered sensory differences of one object from another. An intensive difference arises when comparing objects as integral formations: how a given object, or their set differs from another object or their set as a whole. In simple cases, the difference between the extensive and the intensive may disappear or be masked. For example, apples can be sorted by a directly observable extensive feature of ripeness, size, worminess, etc., or by an intensive feature, which is the variety of apples - the variety can be reduced to a set of extensive features, but can also be perceived directly, as a holistic image.

When it comes to psychological features, many of them, being factors of higher orders than zero, cannot be considered sensorily perceptible. Courage or timidity, egoism or altruism, caution or riskiness are assessed as a holistic feature of an object based on observation and assessment of a set of extensive features associated with human behavior. The holistic image of an object is very specific and can hardly be unambiguously expressed by one word, behind which stands one or another scientific concept, although it can certainly be designated by some word, like a name.

-----------

I will now move from the complexity of differentiating features to identifying general principles to construct a limited set of psychological features that distinguish socionic types from each other.

All psychologically significant differentiating features are, in essence, either elementary or generalized character traits. As was shown in the article, the set of differentiating features, or character traits, is dual in relation to the set of types built on them.

Deductively, the set of differentiating features can be determined by contrasting antisymmetric octaves. If, for example, we contrast all extroverts with all introverts, then the feature of extroversion-introversion will be specified (not defined!) This feature will be considered as an atomic intensity described in words of synonymous forms, with an essence that exists as an intensive difference between all extroverts and all introverts.  According to its primary nature, it has no gradations. Extroversion-introversion is not a scale, it is two poles, two opposite states.

Either one or the other. This feature can be masked, leveled out by other personality traits, so that the impression of greater or lesser extroversion or introversion, and even ambiversion can be constantly created. This is an example of quantum fixation of the state of the psyche. Such a concept can be used only on the assumption that the substrate of the psyche is a certain energy-information field, and mental realities are quanta or resonances of this field, that is, its stable configurations, between which there is no continuous transition, and thus their set is discrete.

Apparently, the same is true for all the other socionic features identified by Reinin and Ausra.  These are fifteen differentiating features known in socionics, but to them it is necessary to add another, non-differentiating or, more precisely, 0-differentiating feature associated with the existence of an object (the Karpenko-Churyumov feature).

Te/Ti, Fe/Fi, Se/Si or Ne/Ni features should be understood as intensive and not graduated.  The position of information aspects in the structure of the "A" model ensures its contribution to the behavior of a particular person. Thus, the integral behavior of a person is a superposition of the contributions of each function, because of which the effect of a greater or lesser degree of expression of the archetypal property may arise. And on this basis, it is possible to organize a diagnostic procedure to identify how much a feature is manifested, but still such manifestation is an indirect indication of the position of information aspects in the structure of the psyche.

The point here is not just the degree, but also the quality of manifestation. Quantitatively, information aspects can be manifested to different degrees simply because the corresponding function has been trained during life or, on the contrary, has not been trained, but the quality of its manifestation will be different depending on what position it occupies in the structure of the psyche of a particular person.

For example, an ILE woman can be a ballerina and achieve great success, since ILE are very hard-working and do not spare effort in training. Using intuition, they can create highly artistic images, making them exceptionally lifelike, but at the same time, they will have some kind of limit, breadth of generalization and, most likely, a very subtly played out element of detachment, spiritual enlightenment, and aspiration to the highest limits.

EIE in a similar case will create a dramatic image, emotionally saturated, with a touch of tragedy, which will not leave anyone indifferent.  In ESE, along with drama and emotional intensity, the character he creates will have a noticeable vitality and stamina.

Yet in IEI, the image will be imbued with subtle lyricism and, depending on the plot, either sad, causing acute sympathy, or foolishly cheerful, which will make even the coolest guy’s smile. And on the contrary, if by force of circumstances IEI becomes a programmer or mathematician, then he will be able to work quite effectively in these areas, using his strong functions. Of course, he will also use routine operations when writing programs, but he will have a desire to find his own, original way to do this work, and an element of treating them as a work of art will appear. In mathematics, he can discover new theorems and create new theories, but they will either be extremely original and so far ahead of their time that not everyone will be able to understand them at once, and he will be almost unable to explain them, since, most likely, he will invest in them a completely different meaning from that which will be discovered in them later, or, being works of “logical” art, they may turn out to be beautiful and very plausible artifacts with which the author will find it very difficult to part. If IEI makes such a discovery, it will happen easily and spontaneously, and in the future, he will try to bring his brainchild to the consciousness of as many people as possible, and he will do this with inspiration and inventively and at every opportunity - at seminars, conferences, including international ones, at various courses, etc. And yet it may turn out that what he spread around himself with such enthusiasm will not stand the test of time and will turn out to be untenable from a scientific point of view.

Differentiating features acquire concreteness when they are related to their position in the model, otherwise they remain approximate abstractions, belonging to the category of vague concepts. Thus, we can talk about eight qualitative gradations of the differentiating feature. We can also assume that extroversion and introversion as features represent the sum of extroversions and introversions associated with the corresponding functions. Thus, the extroversion of extroverts consists of the extroversions of the first, third, sixth and eighth functions. 

One can compare the extroverted tendencies between two extroverts.  For example, the extroverted emotionality of ESE will be more demonstrative than the extroverted intuition of ILE. The same can be said about the extroverted sensorics of ESE in comparison with the extroverted sensorics of ILE. Therefore, ESE can be perceived as initially more extroverted, although each atomic component of extroversion within each specific carrier will differ in its own intensity.

If we take the full extroversion of such an introvert as SEI, it will look extroverted in the second, forth, fifth and seventh functions.  The bearer of such a TIM in his emotional manifestations will look much more demonstrative than ILE, and when comparing them by the manifestation of emotionality, it may seem that SEI is an extrovert, and the ILE is an introvert. However, we should not talk about greater or lesser demonstrativeness of individual functions, but about the holistic attitude of the bearer of the type, then levels of introversion-extroversion will be determined not by external manifestations, but by the parameters of the Base function. The same can be said about rationality-irrationality and all other typological characteristics.

At different times, several socionics (Reinin, Shepetko, Gut) suggested that in addition to the Reinin dichotomies, there should be other features associated with the opposition of other groups of socionic types to each other. So, one could talk about a very extensive set of Reinin-Shepetko-Gut features. Of course, the problem of meaningful interpretation of these features remains. It is not at all easy to intuitively see which feature should be determined by the opposition of the octaves of extroverts and introverts, if, for example, ILE and SEI are swapped in them.  It would be difficult to give a final solution to the problem posed in this chapter in this work - a large team and many scientists should work on it. However, here we can outline some promising approaches to its solution.

The Reinin dichotomies are not simple properties of the psyche, but correspond to the archetypes behind them, generalized concepts, which cannot be unambiguously expressed in commonly used words.

We can try to interpret them, but this is not at all easy. A remarkable example of the complexity of explaining psychological concepts is the case of extroversion and introversion. Jung did not give definitions of these concepts, but only tried to somehow explain and discuss them. Such remarkable psychologists as Eysenck, Cattell, Guilford and many others after them began to use these terms, but as it turned out, they associated them with quite different concepts in a way that seemed right to them. Thus, the totality of the uses of these words by different authors is an unconscious case of homonymy, that is, the same words are used, but the meaning is different. So, it is high time for psychology to put its conceptual economy in order.

In the same way, attempts to directly project such Reinin dichotomies as statics-dynamics, stubborn-compliant, quest-declarative, strategy-tactics, etc. onto concepts known in psychology look, at the very least, naive.

First, let us pay attention to the levels of commonality of features. Signs, one of the poles of which is necessarily present in any person (excluding pathological cases), we will call universal or typological.

Signs that distinguish a relatively small group of people in connection with their professional, ethnic, cultural, pathological, and similar features, we will call local. Signs that distinguish an individual person, contrasting him with the rest of humanity, we will call private.

The features that appear and disappear in a specific person depending on the conditions in which he finds himself, we will call situational. Now we can ask the question, do the terms that Ausra used to designate the objectively existing typological features of the Reinin dichotomies correspond to the features of this level or are there local, private, and situational features behind them? I do not see any theoretical sense in dividing the Reinin dichotomies into primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary, just as D. Lytov does, since I believe that all these features are single level, in the sense as defined above. Therefore, I will consider them all in a row, as it turns out in an ordered system of the Reinin Dichotomies.

A set-theoretic description of a feature is possible when the feature can be presented because of operations on sets, at least disjunctions, conjunctions, and negations.

We can talk about the spectrum of a feature. All general names of features expressed in words should be presented in the form of a conceptual spectrum. For example, the concept "brave" as a differentiating feature has the disadvantage that it is vague. Brave can mean not timid, or it can mean recklessly courageous, or it can approach the meaning of daring. A person can be brave in battle but be timid in the presence of a loved one. Greedy, stingy, stingy, economical, thrifty, calculating, thrifty - a set of concepts behind which there is a generalized feature, opposed to frivolity and thoughtlessness in handling material values.

Decomposition of a feature into semantic factors. In fact, this is what Osgood's idea boils down to - representing a concept as related to the basic coordinate axes of the phase space. But this case can be considered as a limiting one, when any concepts are represented in the same basis. This is the limiting level of generalization of the concept of a semantic factor.

A feature can be considered as a binary structure. In this case, not a single concept should be considered as a feature, but a pair of polarly related concepts, as is the case with the Reinin dichotomies.  In socionics, a feature is always a polar pair.

Like the Reinin features, attributed to the set of sixteen socionic types, we can talk about features attributed to the set of 8 information aspects.  Accordingly, there will be seven of them (and with the unifying feature of existence - eight). This work, at least in part, was done by V.V. Gulenko, and it will be natural to call them by his name - Gulenko features.

At present, I am working on the analysis of even more general groups of features, so the field of work here is quite extensive.

The principle of duality of type and relationship that I put forward can well be applied to the set of Reinin features. Thus, the features can and should be attributed to Jung's (or any other) axes, which makes it possible, firstly, to represent them in the system of these axes, and secondly, to build a model of the feature, which means that it will be possible to work with the feature on the same methodological basis as with TIM. Work in this direction is underway.

We will show that the set of Reinin features is strictly ordered, if we consider the set of socionic types to be strictly ordered too, for example, as it is done in the Lyashkyavichyus table with Churyumov's amendment.

Let's consider the Reinin feature table, as it was filled in by Ausra, changing only the form of presentation, denoting features with numbers, and their poles with plus and minus signs. Then we get table 6.01.

Table 6.01 shows there is no regularity in the pattern of distribution of feature poles between types.  However, Reinin’s idea that the socion and the set of features that determine the difference between types represent an algebraic group due to the relative simplicity and internal symmetry of these objects assumes a regular pattern of features.

Such a regularity is achieved using the Cayley transformation describes by the following algorithm:

1) In a rectangular 15x16 table, select the middle column and from the top to the middle inclusive, put eight pluses (or other signs denoting polarity), and fill the remaining cells in this column with minuses.

2) in the middle column of the left half of the table, put four pluses and four minuses and extend this same configuration to the lower part of this column.

3) of the three remaining left columns, fill the middle one with alternating pairs of plus and minus signs.

4) fill the leftmost column with alternating plus and minus signs.

5) now fill all right columns, symmetrical with respect to the previously filled middle columns, so that the upper halves of the columns are filled identically, and the lower halves are inverted, that is, minuses are put in place of pluses and vice versa.

This construction of the table is purely algebraic in nature and has nothing to do with intuitive amateur arbitrariness!  As a result, we will get a pattern of signs as in table 6.02

If in this table we do not pay attention to the first row, filled with pluses, then we can notice that the remaining part will be symmetrical relative to the left diagonal.  For the entire table together with the first row to become symmetrical relative to the left diagonal, we need to add a zero-column filled with pluses. Obviously, the feature represented by this column is not a distinguishing, differentiating feature, but if the identity of two types is considered as a minimal or zero difference, then everything falls into place, and in the group of features we get a group unit.

In terms of content, this 0 feature can be interpreted as existence, since this is the only thing that is common to all types. The introduction of such a feature is interesting and meaningful from an ontological point of view, since to consider and compare something with another, it must exist.  Let's add a zero feature to table 6.02 and get table 6.03.

The last column of Table 6.03 contains the Intertype relations in the order of their correspondence to the types. Since, based on the duality principle, one can assume a one-to-one correspondence between types and features, the same correspondence can be assumed between features and intertype relations (but this, of course, still needs to be argued!).

Since in Table 6.03 the arrangement of features is reduced to their group-theoretical canonical form, one can assume that it is in this order that the features correspond to the types and intertype relations. In order that overly frivolous critics are not tempted to qualify further reasoning as an adaptation of explanations to a theoretical construct invented on the occasion, let us first try to find at least heuristic arguments in favor of such a correspondence. In this form, the structural similarity of quadra structures and of the types within the quadras are clearly visible. The identification of such regularities suggests that the semantics of archetypes is closely related to their deep structure. In addition, the identity of feature type structures from one quadra makes any movement of types between quadras impossible.

The zero attribute is easy to compare with ILE, as the beginning, the starting point. Not everyone will agree with this, believing that any type can be put in this place, and ILE ended up there only because the creator of socionics coincidentally  turned out to be the bearer of this type. However, this idea will become more plausible if we consider that ILE is structurally compared to the identical relation, which, of course, is natural to accept as the initial one.  This is more logical to do since the identical transformation in algebraic groups corresponds to one in a multiplicative group.

--------------------------------------

It is quite natural to compare SEI with the trait of extroversion-introversion - this is the first introvert in the socion and this is the most extroverted introvert, so in this type the poles of this trait are well contrasted and compared.

It is easy to contrast the intuitive principle with the sensory one in LII in which sensorics is in the weakest positions.

Similarly, it is easy to compare the logic-ethics feature with the IEI - an ethical type in which both logical functions are in weak positions, and, in addition, ethics is "sharpened" by introversion and intuition.

Also, the correspondence between the semantic fields of rationality-irrationality and the LSE, a type that is considered the most rational in socionics, can be assessed as satisfactory.

The arguments presented increase the plausibility of the proposed hypothesis about the existence of a one-to-one correspondence between TIM, Reinin dichotomy and Intertype relation. If such a correspondence really exists, it would be a good help for additional clarification of the semantics and integral image of both types and intertype relation, on the one hand, and Reinin features, on the other.

Accepting the hypothesis put forward as true and keeping in mind the correspondence between EII and the statics-dynamics feature, we can, for example, evaluate EII's type as the most static, or one in which statics is maximally opposed to dynamics. On the other hand, the statics-dynamics feature should be somewhat "similar" to EII. We can say that these objects have the same archetype, but it is realized in different semantic fields. The same archetype should also be present in the intertype relation "control" (Supervision), and then we can consider that control is the maximally static relation.

However, it is useful to evaluate the terms "statics-dynamics" from the point of view of their globality. It seems that, just as a specific person, a bearer of any of the types, can be a decent person and a scoundrel, a hero and a traitor, an honest person, and a criminal, etc., in the same way any person, depending on the situation, can be motionless, for example, at a combat post, or move quickly, escaping pursuit.

However, judging by the descriptions, Ausra did not mean this, and therefore somewhat deformed the semantic field of these concepts. Ausra's terms should be considered preliminary designations of difficult-to-formalize concepts behind specific configurations of the "A" model. Ausra associated the concept of statics with the position in the mental ring of a specific type of aspects. The course of her thought is not difficult to understand, since the aspects Ne and Se define the image of the goal, and the aspects Ti and Fi determine the logical and relational evaluation of these goals. The concept of the dynamics of Ausra relates to the position in the mental ring of a specific type of aspects Te, Ni, Fe, Si. And this is also understandable, since the aspects Te and Fe define the means to achieve the goal, and the aspects Ni and Si determine the time and pragmatic parameters of these means.

However, Ausra did not forget that the vital ring of the "static" is dynamic, while that of the "dynamic" is static. The combination of these semantics leads to the need to interpret such combinations as "the dynamic's desire for a goal is distinguished by staticity" and "the static's goal setting is dynamic." The first of these combinations can be interpreted as "assertiveness", that is, a stable, unshakable desire to achieve a result. The second combination can be understood as, for example, the static's readiness to change his goal in accordance with changing circumstances. Such an interpretation allows us to look at the terms proposed by Ausra in a completely different way. However, it is not so easy to find a replacement for them.

Based on the proposed hypothesis, it is possible to use the relatively more well-known and understandable semantics of TIMs and intertype relations to clarify such difficult-to-interpret features, which Ausra intuitively assigned the names 1) “Carefree-prudent”, 2) “Democrats-aristocrats”, 3) “Stubborn-compliant”, 4) “Merry-serious”, 5) “Left-right”, 6) “Determined-reasonable” (aka Decisive-judicious), and also to check the correspondence of the semantics of the remaining terms used by Ausra to designate Reinin dichotomies.

Thus, the feature “Carefree-prudent” (aka Carefree-farsighted), according to the hypothesis, should correspond to the ESE and the “activation” intertype relation. It should follow from this that the ESE pole of this feature should be optimistic, major, life-affirming, associated with everyday thoroughness, a high level of comfort, and activation of activity. However, the chosen words only set the image of the feature, indicate the archetype behind it, but cannot be used directly for its terminological designation.

The "Left-Right" trait should correspond to the SEE and the "superego" attitude. The mysterious word "superego" feels like something connected with a position of power, something based on personal superiority. But socionics represent the semantic field of Se quite well. This type is very strong and at the same time able to be charming when necessary. Certainly, powerful, but achieving his goals not only by direct pressure, but also by the ability to quickly establish emotional contacts. He feels the attitude towards himself well and knows how to change it in his favor by any means, including persuasion, threats, promises and blackmail. He understands intrigue, knows how to speak beautifully, never stops at what others would consider a lie, and if he lies and boasts, he does it very artistically and completely identifies with what is being discussed, so that it is difficult for the interlocutor to suspect deception. If he is exposed, he, without a twinge of conscience and depending on the circumstances, turns everything into a joke and calmly laughs or snaps back angrily. To achieve his goal, he stops at nothing. On the EII, he gives the impression of a shameless "outlaw". Let us also remember that in socionics, for the informal designation of this TIM, a successful, in my opinion, term "Politician" (V.V. Gulenko) was proposed.  It is obvious that the semantic field of the concept "Politician" is in good agreement with the semantic field of TIM Se.

Based on such a (partial) description of the semantic field of this type, one can form an idea of ​​the "superego" relationship. People in such a relationship involuntarily make a strong irrational impression on each other, which simultaneously attracts and alarms, a complex mental and psychological game unfolds between the partners, in which each seeks to appear important, significant and to use the partner to achieve their goals, using hints, promises, unreliable or dubious information. If the partners have common interests, then an unspoken agreement arises between them for the time of achieving the goal, when they, like card players, jealously watch each other and are ready to "throw" each other at any moment. If the partners' interests are opposite, then a very intense irrational conflict flares up between them, during which the partners stop at nothing, touching on the most vulnerable and painful sides of the other, often speaking from the position of the other's conscience, and this is especially difficult for a person to endure.

Now, having an idea of ​​the semantic fields of the corresponding TIM and intertype relations, we can try to form an idea of ​​the semantic field of the feature "Left-Right". Obviously, this feature is associated with very intense manifestations of personality, with a tendency to intrigue, deceit, fundamental mistrust, the desire to achieve one's goals at any cost. This fragment of the description of the hypothetical semantic field of this feature is very reminiscent of the semantic field of political struggle. Thus, the term intuitively chosen by Ausra fully corresponds to the semantics of the feature, reflecting the realities of the political situation - the political inclination of TIM to political "leftism" or "rightism" seems to have typological roots. True, Ausra chose this term based on the TIM's belonging to the left or right ring of order-control.

And this feature is internal - external. That is, the informational aspects of the highest level are expressed through themselves. This is the basis for accepting them as an undefinable axiomatic conceptual basis from which everything else can be deductively derived. However, the above mechanism of folding information aspects can also be used for their unfolding. Then the 16x16 table can easily be unfolded into a 32x32 table, resulting in table 6.12.

Table 6.12 represents information aspect codes of a more detailed level than the 16x16 socionic table, however, the interpretation of these aspects, as well as aspects of even more specific ones, is a problem. The table of hexagrams from the I-Ching can be understood as a set of aspects of the 64x64 level. Of course, such an identification must be specially substantiated.

From this point of view, the absence of 16x16 and 32x32 expansions in Chinese philosophy is a certain problem.

Of course, the expansion of information aspects can be extended to any natural number n = 2N, but the problem is the interpretation of the information aspects presented there. However, it seems that it is along this path that we should seek the development of typology, and not along the path of introducing subtypes. A deeper semantic interpretation of information aspects tables of different levels requires a lot of precise work. Let us hope that soon, with sufficient funding, it will be done.

Any table of aspects can easily be represented in analytical codes, like those shown in tables 6.06 and 6.07.

The mechanisms of folding and unfolding socionic tables can be used for a rigorous mathematical proof of the unambiguous ordering of a socion as a set of TIMs. The scheme of the proof is as follows. We take as a starting point for the construction a minimal table, the structure of which is obvious and does not require proof. We expand it to the required level, and, having selected a specific subject area, we meaningfully interpret the rows of such a table. Such an interpretation will be extensive in nature since it is a list of semantic multipliers of individual + - poles of differentiating features. We construct an integral image of the primary extensive interpretation of the table rows, which will give us an intensive interpretation. The set of intensive interpretations is precisely the set of types of the selected level. If we now compare the semantic field of the first row of the intensive interpretation with the semantic field of the ILE, it will not be difficult to verify their isomorphism. The first line will include only positive poles of differentiating features, and this forms the initial type in the set. Which is what was required to be proven. Of course, anyone who wants to can easily do all the listed operations independently and be convinced of the strict orderliness of the socion.

  

----------------------------

Conclusions on the sixth chapter

1. In psychology there is a problem of differentiating features, which relates to their logical vagueness.

2. Attempts to eliminate the vagueness of the feature led to the development of such methods as the semantic differential (C. Osgood), repertory grids (E. Kelly), etc.

3. Differentiating features acquire concreteness when they are related to the position in the model, otherwise they remain approximate abstractions related to the category of vague concepts.

4. It is possible to identify many differentiating features counting in the hundreds of thousands, which significantly exceeds the volume of psychological dictionaries of national languages. Such features may include Reinin-Shepetko-Gut, Gulenko, and other features, but for such a hypothesis to receive sufficient grounds, it is necessary to prove the presence of semantic potential in arbitrary sections of arbitrary discrete sets.

5. Recommendations for further development of the theory of features are proposed.

6. Based on the duality principle, a hypothesis about a one-to-one correspondence between the sets of TIMs, IOs, and differentiating features is put forward and partially substantiated.

7. An idea about the possibility of creating a feature model is put forward and substantiated, which, presumably, will eliminate their blurriness.

8. A mechanism for unfolding information aspects to any level 2N is proposed, where N is any natural number.

9. Based on the mechanisms of unfolding dichotomous matrices, the THEOREM OF UNIQUE ORDERING OF SOCION AS A SET OF SOCIONIC TYPES has been strictly proven.

**Chapter 7**

**Chapter 7: Mathematical Socionics and Partially Alternative Churyumov Algebra**

The talented mathematician G.R. Reinin’s application of mathematics to socionics gave an unexpected and extremely valuable result.  Having made a mathematical proof of J. Ekman's formula on the ratio of the number of types in typology differentiating features – n: n = N - 1, Reinin informed Ausra that, along with the four Jungian differentiating features, there should be 11 more differentiating features, so that their total number should be 15.  Reinin, limited himself to mathematical abstractions, and did not propose a meaningful algorithm for assigning traits to psychological types.

Ausra, with all her socionic enthusiasm, immediately spent 2 weeks in the complex search for these traits, finding antisymmetric octaves describing their supposed semantics, and giving them conditional preliminary names. There were exactly 15 such octaves by the number of traits, although it was not necessary to assume this in advance, since it would be possible, for example, that one and the same trait could be provided by different groups of octaves. Ausra showed that the first case takes place, which, together with her development of the semantics of the Reinin traits, gives grounds to name the 15 pairs of octaves she found. In honor of Reinin's initiative, she called the traits she found Reinin's traits. Of course, this was her copyright, and it was fair in connection with Reinin's successful discovery, but now, after her death, it would be fair to call these traits by the double name "Ausra-Reinin features", understanding her invaluable contribution to the development of the semantics of this construct.

Why the neutral feature (or trait) of “existence” creates a 16th Reinin Dichotomy:

Reinin, being a talented mathematician, made the calculations quite correctly, but he did not attach importance to the fact that an algebraic group must necessarily contain a single, or neutral feature.  This feature does not contrast anything, which, in a mathematical sense, can be considered a 0-contrast. A neutral feature is distinguished by the fact that it is inherent in all elements of the group.  Such a feature is “existence” - any object, including a feature, must exist before possessing any parameters. 

When working with the Reinin Dichotomy table, I originally assumed that there were exactly 15 Reinin features or traits, but when trying to find their strict mathematical order, I concluded that it was necessary to add a 16th, neutral feature, without which the table could not be symmetrized.  Later I will show that the neutral element corresponds to a specific psychological meaning, which is a sufficient argument not to neglect it.

35 Small Groups

Reinin's work on groups of fours, the semantics of which is determined by linearly dependent triples of the Reinin features, turned out to be very interesting and at the same time unexpected. Reinin mathematically proved that there are exactly 35 such triples, and, accordingly, there are also 35 groups of fours associated with them, and the fours themselves are 140. The set of these fours has rightly become entrenched in the minds of socionics as "Reinin's correct fours". Having chosen the poles of the basic features or traits as a generalized coordinate basis, Reinin showed how, by combining them, one can obtain components of the derived features or traits.

Reinin demonstrated that combining 2 separate dichotomies (X & Y) with 2 binary +/- poles reveals a third dichotomy (Z) of 4 fours.

Example: X + Y = Z

X = Extrovert (-x) / Introvert (+x)

Y = Intuitive (-y) / Sensory (+y)

Z = Carefree (-x-y & +x+y) / Farsighted (-x+y & +x-y)

------------------------------------------------------------------

Also true:  Y + Z = X   /   X + Z = Y

Thus, Reinin showed that any 3 Reinin dichotomies form 3 interchangeable algebraic groups.  

So:

X (Intuitive) + Y (Logical) = Z (Aristocratic)

X (Intuitive) + Z (Aristocratic) = Y (Logical)

Y (Logical) + Z (Aristocratic) = X (Intuitive)

----------------------------------------------------------------------

A one-to-one relationship can be established between TIM and ITR.  This can be done in different ways, but here we use set-theoretic operations.  To do this, TIM can be expressed through Reinin trait - this will result in a 16-bit code that defines the full attribute structure of TIM, but for practical purposes it is quite possible to get by with expressing TIM through the poles of the Jungian basis, i.e. through extroversion / introversion, irrationality / rationality, intuition / sensorics and logic / ethics, replacing each of the poles of these polar constructs, respectively, with 1 or 0, and arranging them in the same order. If we take any TIM in this MC.01 table and compare its TIM code with ILE's TIM code - in logic this operation is called equivalence, replacing the same digits with one and different ones with zero, then we will get the intertype relation code of the corresponding relation - in this case, between ILE and the selected TIM. This is shown in the last column of the table.  Here we are not talking about binary number digits - this is a positional code.  We are talking about a certain composition that has a meaningful objective meaning, namely: firstly, here the sign markers (not numbers!) occupy strictly defined places corresponding to the systemic structure of the socion with its mathematically proven strict orderliness, and these markers indicate the poles of the Reinin trait; and, secondly, the meaning of such a comparison is that the identity of the corresponding poles is affirmed or denied, and, therefore, the degree of difference of generalized cognitive positions, which can be understood as a highly abstract component of interhuman relations, as a result of which one of two varieties of socionic relations is set.  The selected type of relations (IR) allows us to draw conclusions related to all TIMs, based on the conclusions about the relations of all TIMs to the TIM of ILE.

The coincidence of the codes of TIM and ITR is an indicator of their substantive isomorphism, since their semantics is determined by the same poles of the Reinin trait, which allows us to put the elements of these two sets in a one-to-one correspondence. From a symbolic point of view, the relationship is a difference in cognitive positions, which can be assessed as a composition of dichotomous codes - complete or reduced to one or another basis, the simplest, of course, to Jung's. Naturally, the composition of the comparison of positions turned out to be adequate: if the signs in one position coincide, then this substantive means that both types have the same corresponding polarity, which can be interpreted as the degree of approximation to identity, and in the opposite case - as the degree of deviation from it. Having expressed the TIM through the Reinin trait, we obtain highly generalized structural formulas in Table MC.03.  A table of this kind was first constructed by Ausra, however, the arrangement of the Reinin trait was motivated by random circumstances that depended on Ausra's choice of the sequence of polar octaves. Later, I mathematically proved the unambiguous ordering of TIMs in the socion and Reinin traits in the structure of the TIM, which this table presents.

This table expresses not two, but six relations:  1) TIM-Reinin trait, 2) Reinin trait-TIM, 3) TIM-ITR, 4) ITR-TIM, 5) Rein trait-ITR, 6) ITR-Reinin trait, and, thus, exhausts the set of relations between these TIM, Reinin trait and ITR.  These relations allow us to hypothesize that not only the set of Reinin traits, but also the sets of TIM and ITR are also algebraic groups.  As proof, we represent each row of the Reinin traits, i.e. the structural codes of the TIM, as conditional numbers in the binary number system.  Performing the set-theoretic equivalence operation on any pair from this set, we obtain one of the codes from the same set.

ILE and Identity have a common semantic factor, which should be used as a criterion when assessing their concretized meanings. Thus, ILE and Identity have a common theme of fundamentality. To exist means to preserve something that remains identical to itself, which is a fundamental property of existence. Identity is the primary property of being, which is the most fundamental ontological essence.  We find the same theme in ILE - the focus on discovering the fundamental laws of nature. 

Based on this heuristic principle, we need to look for ways to clarify other, insufficiently clarified Reinin traits, since TIMs and ITRs, in the first approximation, turned out to be more accessible for semantic identification. Thus, for example, ESE and the corresponding ITR “Activation” have their own models and can be described with a sufficient degree of validity according to them. At the same time, the corresponding Reinin trait Carefree-Farsighted has no sufficient grounds to be considered literally coinciding in meaning with the meaning of the words denoting it.  However, it must have such themes as extroversion, rationality, sensory and emotionality, as well as activity.  Similar reasoning applies to all other Reinin traits, including, and to such relatively more understandable ones as extroversion and introversion, although it would be a mistake to simplify their content, reducing it, for example, to openness-closedness, sociability-isolation, greater energy, less energy, etc.  By establishing algebraic relations between the elements of the sets TIM, ITR and Reinin trait, we also get the opportunity to make formal substitutions in the corresponding formulas, thereby gaining access to more subtle socionic meanings.

As for the idea of ​​the existence of 16 socions (if I am not mistaken, G. Chikiris was the first to express it), it is certainly beautiful, but it is certainly impossible to accept it without detailed argumentation. Behind this idea is a simple thought that any other type can be put in first place in a socion instead of ILE. And, perhaps, this is quite democratic. But, perhaps, it is unlawful to demand democracy, for example, in the structure of chemical molecules. Let's say we demand that "democratic" justice be restored in the water molecule by adding one more oxygen atom, so that the formula is not H2O, but H2O2. We can demand it, but it will be a completely different substance (hydrogen peroxide). Therefore, in the structure of a socion, we must proceed from its law, which, of course, must be discovered, and not invented.

Variations within type

I managed to prove mathematically that a socion is a strictly ordered set, where each TIM stands in its place, and nothing can be rearranged there - like in a water molecule. Nevertheless, the idea of ​​​​multiplicity of socions (subtypes) has some grounds. Namely, ethnic groups and states have their typological shades, and this means that the same type will obviously feel differently in different ethnic groups, but this is not a matter of changing the socion, but of a different psychological environment. This is like how relationships are built between types - with different types in different ways.

For example, the ILE type will feel differently in Russia (IEI), England (LSE) or Germany (LSI).  In Russia, the people treat this type of people with tolerance, sympathy and understanding. But the Russian authorities (SLE) are in a passive antagonism (Superego) attitude towards this type of people. This means that they do not encourage them but can take advantage of their openness.  In England, the authorities treat ILEs from the position of active synergy - they expect results from this type of people that could form the basis of new technologies.  Here science, the TIM of which as a social infrastructure of ILE, is supported by the state. While in Russia science is financed on a residual basis and depends on the "favor" of government officials, which leads to a high level of corruption in science, in particular, the presence of non-scientific ballast in it, attached "by connections" to "bread and butter" positions.  In Germany, this type of people and the corresponding infrastructures are in the position of socionic controllers, which ensures increased rigor for the reliability of scientific results. The above discussion shows that in developing a theory it is necessary to rely not only on intuition, but also to use logic.

Letter from Ausra to the author:

  

Semyon, I received all your letters, except for the first one, thank you.

As for the interpretations of Superid, they are very superficial and random for me.  You just need to look at the elements that make up Superid. 

Yes, ILE strives to improve his mood, but, in fact, it's the other way around, it's SEI who strives to improve his mood, because the emotionally unwound ILE is, on the one hand, completely demobilized, and on the other, angry and angry precisely because of his lack of emotionality. But emotionality is lacking when there is not enough variety of pleasant and unpleasant sensations, he himself strives only for pleasant sensations, because of which he can completely demobilize. But SEI tells him - get into cold water, then it will be pleasant. In general, SEI provides him with the unpleasant sensations necessary for the activity of the organism, and this taken together gives an emotional upsurge, in fact - a certain physical excitement. Because SUPERID is somatic.

As for EIE, he knows perfectly well what he needs. But not what he does not need.  This knowledge of what is unnecessary and salvation from unnecessary objects is what LSI is engaged in.  This in turn provides mobilization and energy, that is - extroverted sensorics of EIE. Otherwise, he is sluggish and demobilized.  Approximately the same with the SUPERID of all types of information metabolism.
